maintopic: DELEGATION ON FAR EASTERN SITUATION AND REELECTION OF SPAIN TO COUNCIL
DELEGATION ON FAR EASTERN SITUATION AND REELECTION OF SPAIN TO COUNCIL
speechtext:
1.	Did Canada's League of Nations delegation at Geneva vote on October 6, 1937, on the report of the drafting committee of the League of Nations, recommending that signatories of the Nine Power Treaty be invited to meet to examine the far eastern situation?
2.	What instruction or advice was given to the Canadian delegation by the government of Canada or the Department of External Affairs on or about September 20, 1937, regarding the question of the reelection of Spain to a seat on the council of the League of Nations?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DELEGATION ON FAR EASTERN SITUATION AND REELECTION OF SPAIN TO COUNCIL
speechtext:
Hon. members will see that this question is really two questions, and both involve matters on which there has been a good deal of misunderstanding, but neither question is so framed that an answer limited to the point raised would be of much assistance in making the situation clear. I therefore propose to answer the question orally and in the form of a statement on the questions referred to.
The first question refers to press reports last October to the effect that the Canadian delegation in the league assembly had abstained from voting on the resolution regarding the Sino-Japanese war, and to the effect further that this was due to failure on the part of the Canadian government to send instructions promptly.
The Sino-Japanese conflict was referred by the assembly to a committee termed the far eastern advisory committee, on which Canada was represented. Some phases of the question were referred by this committee to a subcommittee on which Canada was not represented, and this subcommittee finally

Questions
set up a drafting committee. The drafting committee reached agreement on the text of a report on the afternoon of October 5. An attempt was made to rush the report through the three remaining stages that same day, regardless of the consideration that a large number of members of the assembly were not represented on the sub-committee or on the committee itself. After adoption by the subcommittee it was referred to the full committee. The senior Canadian representative quite properly refrained from voting, giving his reasons as follows:
This is the first time I have seen the two reports under discussion. I notice that they contain conclusions of great importance. I have no instructions from my government, to which I would at least like to communicate the conclusions with a view to obtaining their approval as soon as possible. Therefore, in the circumstances, I am bound to suspend my adhesion to these reports until such time as I have received these instructions. I hope they will be available before the matter is discussed by the assembly, when I hope that I shall be able to support the reports.
Later in the same evening, at eight-thirty, the report was sent on to the assembly, and it was proposed to proceed immediately with the discussion and voting. The delegates of Norway and the Union of South Africa protested that they had had no time to study the report and resolution or communicate with their governments. It was agreed to adjourn to the following afternoon.
The Canadian delegation at once cabled the resolution and their own views. That telegram was received and decoded at ten o'clock in the morning and delivered to me personally at once. The procedure adopted left no opportunity for consulting my colleagues, as it was then three p.m. in Geneva, but I concluded, in view of previous discussions and the tenor of the resolution, that no material question would arise, and therefore directed that a cable be sent in reply authorizing the Canadian delegation to support the resolution. This cable was dispatched in an hour and a quarter after the cable from Geneva had been received and decoded in the department. I brought the question before my colleagues at the first opportunity. When the reports and the resolution based on them came before the assembly that afternoon the Canadian delegation gave its support. No formal vote was taken. The procedure adopted was a negative one, which seems to be growing in use at Geneva, of considering all delegations present as supporting, unless voting contrary or declaring that they abstain. Two of the delegations present, Poland and Siam, abstained. It will thus be seen that there was no delay whatever at Ottawa, and that the Canadian
delegation at Geneva was entirely justified in declining to vote on a resolution on a matter of first importance without having had adequate opportunity to consult the Canadian government. No other course would be possible if the work of the league is to be taken seriously and if members at a distance from Europe are to take a considered and responsible part in its deliberations.
The second query has to do with the voting on a question of lesser importance, namely, the election of members of the council.
Members of the house will recall that in addition to the permanent or great power members of the council, now reduced to Great Britain, France and Russia, and also Italy, which has announced its resignation, it is the practice to elect temporary members, usually for a three year term. Certain countries have developed claims in the past ten years to semipermanent seats. Before any temporary member which is retiring can be considered fol reelection the rules provide that it must obtain from' the assembly a declaration of re-eligibility by a two-thirds vote. If successful it may then be a candidate for reelection. On the present occasion Spain and Turkey failed to secure the necessary majority for reeligibility. The countries elected in place of Chile, Spain and Turkey were Belgium, Iran (formerly Persia) and Peru.
As to Canadian instructions, none were given on this occasion and none have been given for some years past. The full list of candidates is not known until the assembly is in session. I may add that information on every phase of the assembly agenda, to the extent of some hundred pages, was furnished the members of the delegation, and some points of special importance were discussed in council before the Canadian delegation left.
Following the vote the Geneva correspondent of an English paper telegraphed that the empire delegates had split on the question of Spanish re-eligibility; Canada, the Irish Free State, India and Egypt voting against Spain's re-eligibility, and the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand for it. This irresponsible statement was relayed to Canada by two Canadian correspondents in London, and in due course various editorials and resolutions appeared criticizing the alleged stand. Not one of the critics appeared to have stopped to consider whether the report could have any foundation, or what the league procedure was in such voting. The fact is that under article 2 of the rules adopted by the assembly for the election of non-permanent members it is provided:
The assembly shall pronounce separately by secret ballot upon each request for re-eligibility.
Questions

I need only say that the correspondent who sent out this story had no information or facts whatever to base the story upon. It was an irresponsible cable, based upon guess or gossip. The Canadian delegation did not give any statement as to its vote.
I am not aware that any responsible country has ever made a statement as to how its delegation voted on a question which the league assembly had expressly provided should be balloted upon in secret. The secrecy imposed upon such balloting is a league regulation, not a Canadian decision. To break this rule because a Geneva correspondent sends out reports on subjects of which he has no knowledge would simply encourage the circulation of guesswork in the hope of provoking a denial or confirmation. For this reason, at the time the dispatches appeared, I felt it desirable and necessary to refrain from indicating how the Canadian delegation voted. I intimated, however, at the time that 1 thought it might be possible, in the event of the matter being brought up in parliament, to give to parliament the information sought. As the question has been asked, and a refusal to give the information requested might only lead to renewed controversy and misrepresentation of Canada's position, I have decided to inform the house what in fact was the action taken by the Canadian delegation in this case. I am not sure that in so doing I am justified under the league regulations. I hope however that my so doing may serve to emphasize the necessity for avoiding reckless news stories and unconsidered comment on questions which easily arouse acrimony and friction, and also do something to prevent similar incidents in future.
The Canadian delegation voted for the reeligibility of Spain. The reasons why the Canadian delegation voted for the re-eligibility of Spain are very concisely set forth in a letter which I received from Senator Dandu-rand shortly after the vote was recorded. It is dated Brussels, November 10, 1937, and is as follows:
The Right Hon. The Prime Minister,
Secretary of State for External Affairs, Ottawa, Ontario.
My Hear Prime Minister,
I have taken cognizance of the debate which has taken place in the Canadian press over the attitude of the Canadian delegation in relation to the request of Spain to be again allowed to present its candidature for a seat in the council of the league. The query repeatedly made to you bore on the vote which Canada gave on that question. You answered quite properly that the vote had been taken by secret ballot and that the public was not made aware of the way in which the various nations had recorded their will.
IMr. Mackenzie King.]
I may say that to this date I am unaware as to the individual action of the members of the league. I do not know how Great Britain voted, nor the other members of the commonwealth, although I met them daily.
Since you stated publicly that you would give that information to parliament, if it were asked and if you were allowed to by the rules governing the assembly of the league of nations, I have no hesitation whatever in informing you that the Canadian delegation voted in favour of the re-eligibility of Spain, for the following reasons:
1.	When Spain expressed in 1926 its intention of withdrawing from the League of Nations, if the assembly did not allow her a permanent seat in the council, it was suggested that an opportunity would be afforded of obtaining election to a non-permanent seat, with the right of re-eligibility on a two-thirds vote. Two years later, in 1928, the same procedure was proposed again. In order to secure the collaboration of Spain in the work of the league, a resolution to that effect was carried in the assembly by a vote of 44 to 5. Canada supported the resolution.
2.	Because the Canadian delegation did not feel that the calamity of war in Spain could justify the members of the league to inflict upon this unhappy country the further humiliation of the loss of its seat in the council;
3.	Because the Canadian delegation had solely Spain in mind, without asking themselves what government would represent her, to-day or to-morrow, in the assembly and in the council;
4.	Because the Canadian delegation could not take sides for one faction or the other, as Canada had faithfully followed the policy of non-intervention in the affairs of Spain.
The sole duty of the Canadian delegation was to think of Spain as an entity, without interfering in its domestic quarrels.
Yours very faithfully,
R. Dandurand.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should place before parliament at an early date plans, or proposals, for a comprehensive and authoritative survey of water conservation, irrigation possibilities, and other feasible projects for the permanent rehabilitation of the drought stricken area of western Canada and its people.
He said: Mr. Speaker, may I first remark that the resolution asks not for the actual undertaking of large scale irrigation projects, but for the consideration of the appointment of an authoritative committee to look into the feasibility of such projects in western Canada.
From time to time in this parliament conditions in western Canada have been outlined, and if further proof were needed of the extent of the disaster which has befallen not only the western provinces but the entire dominion, it could, I think, be found in the submission of the Saskatchewan government to the Rowell commission. Two or three years ago it was quite usual for some public men to pass off conditions somewhat lightly by saying that one or two good crops would meet the situation. I do not think anyone familiar with conditions existing there to-day would contend that one or two crops would meet that situation.
During the past summer the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) and the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) drove over the major portion of the drought area. I drove over it at that time, and again this fall. The picture of devastation one saw was almost indescribable. If one enters Saskatchewan at the southern boundary, from the United States, or at the eastern boundary from the Manitoba border, and drives right across into southern Alberta; thence north to a point just east of Edmonton, thence in a southeasterly direction to about where the main line of the Canadian Pacific railway crosses the Manitoba border, and thence through southwestern Manitoba, he gets an idea of the appalling condition and the huge territory affected by the drought-mile after mile of burnt up vegetation in the summer; mile after mile of black Russian thistle in the fall, a picture which in my opinion is comparable only to that presented by one of the great deserts to be found elsewhere in North America, Indeed, driving over the desert

last summer in the state of Washington, where the Grande Coulee irrigation project was being carried out, I could imagine myself in Saskatchewan, except that the vegetation was sage-brush instead of Russian thistle.
Because of this condition, in recent years there has been a disposition to look into the records, and to inquire if this great western country in past days has been subject to periodic droughts. I have read the reports, as no doubt have other hon. members, of the explorers who crossed the great plains during the middle of the last century, and I have noticed particularly the records left by Captain Palliser and Mr. Hind. These records indicate that in those days there had been prolonged and disastrous dry periods.
For example, at page 11 of his report, Captain Palliser says this:
After leaving the eastern limit of the country that is within the influence of the mountains the south Saskatchewan flows in a deep and narrow valley through a region of arid plains devoid of timber or pasture of good quality. Even on the alluvial points in the bottom of the valley, trees and shrubs only occur in a few isolated patches. The steep and lofty sides of the valley are composed of calcareous marls and clays that are baked into a compact mass under the heat of the parching sun. The sage and the cactus abound, and the whole scanty vegetation bespeaks an arid climate, but at the elbow the same arid description of the country was met with, and it seems certain that this prevails throughout the entire distance.
Then, at page 51 of the same report Palliser speaks of his arrival at Fort Qu'Appelle on September 13, 1858. On September 14, he started towards Moose Jaw creek, and in that connection makes this statement:
Our roads during the early part of to-day was mostly through a country moderately well wooded, over good land, well suited to agricultural purposes where there were also lakes and hay producing swamps, but towards evening, we began to observe symptoms that showed us we were again near the line of desert country, or northern extension of the North American arid basin.
Again, at page 52 of the report, September 15, 1858, he makes this statement:
Our course was due west and, as far as the eye can reach nothing but desolate plains met the views; at noon we reached a small creek called "the creek before the creek where the bones lie"; here we found water and some little grass, also a few willows and cherry bushes, but no wood fit for fuel. In the evening, reached the creek where the bones lie-
Probably that is where Regina now stands.

where we found water and very little grass; a few willows also grew here, but no wood fit for fuel.

Drought Area-Mr. Coldwell
Then, farther down on the page he adds:
We reached the Moose Jaw creek where there was wood and water. Here our Indian, Nichiwa, advised us to bring wood for five nights along in our carts, and told us it was the last we should see between this and the elbow of the south Saskatchewan.
They camped several days later on Thunder Mountain creek, and again his comment of the neighborhood is made in these words at page 54:
The grass in this arid soil, always so scanty, was now actually swept away by the buffalo, who, assisted by the locusts, had left the country as bare as if it has been overrun by fire; even at the edge of Sage creek, we could obtain very little grass for our horses.
I need not quote more from Palliser's report, except to say that from the Elbow north he reports a wooded country, in his opinion well suited to agriculture. The description of the southern area is a description of what is now known as the drought area.
Another traveller, whose narrative is to be found in the parliamentary library, is Henry Youle Hind, M.A., F.R.G.S. He, too, explored the country in 1858, but took a more southerly route in Manitoba, and along the Souris river. At page 297 of volume I, Mr. Hind speaks of the grasshoppers, which usually accompany drought. He says:
Upon one occasion the whole heavens towards the south, east and west, appeared to radiate a soft grey-tinted light with a quivering motion, and the day being calm, the hum produced by the vibration of so many millions of wings was quite indescribable. The aspect of the heavens during the greatest flight we observed, was singularly striking. It produced a feeling of uneasiness, amazement, and awe in our minds, as if some terrible, unforeseen calamity were about to happen.
That was on July 2, 1858. Then, at page 338 he speaks of the difficulty of obtaining wood, and regrets that they carried none with them. He says:
No tree or shrub or even willow twig could be seen in any direction from our camp on the morning of the 25th.
He adds that they went supperless to bed and the customary breakfast of tea and buffalo meat was impossible. This, may I add, was the day after they left Moose Jaw forks. This description of the country before the white settler came would indicate that drought conditions were not unknown in the days when the prairie was covered with thick sod and prairie wool and when the subsoil moisture had not been depleted by the raising of heavy cereal crops. Then came years of settlement which, with intermittent but short dry periods, were years of fairly satisfactory rainfall. Because of this, the dangers ahead were not recognized
by governments or by those interested in the settling of western land.
It should be noted, however, that shortly before the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan were formed in 1905 the then premier of the Northwest Territories, Sir Frederick Haul-tain, who, I am glad to say, is still living, proposed that one province should be formed between the Manitoba boundary and the mountains. He wanted the new province to own and control its own lands and natural resources, and he particularly desired provincial control of southwestern Saskatchewan and southeastern Alberta. Sir Frederick desired to control these lands partly because he wished to retain them as ranching and grazing country. He did not consider them to be suitable for settlement, but a reading of the records would indicate that to a large extent those who wanted to open up these lands for settlement argued that it was the selfish interest of the ranchers that governed Sir Frederick's policy. There are members of this house, particularly the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) and the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell), who will remember this controversy quite well.
At all events two provinces were formed and a new premier was designated for Saskatchewan by the federal Liberal government of the day. In the ensuing provincial general election Sir Frederick Haultain and his provincial rights party were defeated. Old timers in that part of Saskatchewan and Alberta continued to declare that the new settlers and homesteaders who came into that country to break the land would one day be faced with drought and be ruined. History seems to have vindicated their predictions to a regrettable degree. This dominion parliament must take the responsibility for the opening up of this territory for farming operations and, therefore, the rehabilitation of the area should also be a federal responsibility.
The cause of drought in western Canada is not hard to find. As someone said in this house during the debate on the address, it is primarily due to lack of moisture. I draw particular attention to that statement-a lack of moisture, not a lack of rain. In the days when the prairie plains were simply the haunts of Indians and grazing lands for herds of buffalo, the land was covered with short grass which made no great demand upon the stored up moisture in the subsoil. When the snow melted in the spring or when rail fell upon the natural covering, it slowly percolated through the tiny openings in the grass and down into the subsoil where it found storage space. This storage was assisted by the thick sod which from year to year formed and grew thicker,
63S
Drought Area-Mr. Coldwell

thus holding the winter snow and minimizing surface evaporation. When the pioneer settlers took over this unbroken land they found beneath it a rich store of subsoil moisture that had accumulated in this way throughout the ages.
What water ran off at that time ran into depressions to form little sloughs, lakes or marshes, and these together formed a watershed from which through seepage and capillary action the level of the subsoil moisture was kept fairly constant just beneath the prairie sod, except in those periods of prevailing drought such as Palliser indicated in his journal. The destruction of this natural earth covering by the settler's plough and the sowing of crops, together with thick growths of weeds, made greater demands on the stored up moisture than the scanty precipitation could replace in a single year. Even in years of normal rainfall, in many areas the moisture was being used up at a greater rate than it could be replaced. Our western farmers have been accused of using the moisture and the chemical content of the soil at too great a rate, but I believe that as a class the farmers do not desire to deplete their soil which, if I may so put it, is their constant capital. However, what choice have they when long periods of high production at low prices failed to enable them to meet their obligations and the fixed charges of taxes, interest, and so on?
The very tilling of the soil has helped also to make the restoration of moisture more difficult. Soil deficient in vegetable matter sheds water quickly, particularly when it is a clay soil. When raindrops fall upon the fine prairie mulch they make a film which chokes for a time the pores of the soil and the result is the water runs off rapidly. Subsequent hot sunshine bakes the clay surface and cements it. I have studied some very interesting statistics gathered by the department of agriculture in the United States dealing with the loss of moisture through the growing of crops and by the formation of this surface film. In its natural state the prairie sod has millions of tiny openings made by little roots, sometimes made by insects and worms, and the water tends to percolate to the subsoil. But with the breaking of the sod, that was ended to a degree. Previously when the raindrops fell on the natural covering they were broken up and they percolated slowly into the subsoil beneath which they formed a reservoir of moisture for future growth.
I would emphasize that to-day that covering is gone, and the wind swept plains unfortunately are with us. All this would seem to [Mr. Coldwell.)
indicate that if the west is blessed again with a wet year or even with several successive wet years the restoration of subsoil moisture will not be sufficient to withstand the inevitable dry years that will follow. Because of this in my opinion we must consider ways and means of watering the land and filling the empty sloughs and lakes in the drought region and thus restore the table level of subsoil moisture of which in these days we hear so much. Moreover the drought region is extending. This is to be expected, because the intense heat of the dry land dries up land adjacent to it, and the desert tends to extend. Wind erosion follows and dust and the blowing topsoil cause still greater disaster.
There are those who say that irrigation is not feasible because there is a lack of water. But wheat is a semi-arid plant which requires a minimum of moisture provided it receives that moisture at the right time. In several of the recent so-called dry years the annual precipitation has been sufficient to ensure a crop of wheat, but the crop failed because the moisture did not fall at the right time; the subsoil moisture was lacking to carry the crop along. Hence it is not a question of large quantities of water, but of being able to deliver at the right time to the growing crops the comparatively small amount of water often required. For this purpose I believe there is sufficient water in the rivers and streams of western Canada.
A friend of mine last summer, when the days were hot. stood near Saskatchewan landing and watched the south Saskatchewan, incidentally lower than usual, roll by. He told me that the river was in flood-not a great flood such as we have known in the past, but comparatively in flood-at a much higher level than normal last year, and flowing at about eight miles per hour in a channel one-quarter of a mile wide. He estimated that if the water were diverted it would cover many sections of land one foot deep within twenty-four hours.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext: What month was that?

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
That was in July. I
do not know how correct that estimate is, but I do know that vast quantities of water are flowing through the parched lands both from the North and South Saskatchewan rivers to the Arctic seas without being utilized in any way whatever. I have endeavoured to discuss these matters with engineers and others who have looked into the problem;
I have gone carefully over the contour maps of the dried-out area, and as a layman I would say that wide-scale irrigation seems to present

Drought Area-Mr. Coldwell
no insuperable difficulties, either physical or financial, on the northern side of the Mis-souri-Coteau divide. True, some damming might be required, but the height of the land over which the water would have to flow from, let us say, the South Saskatchewan, near River-hurst. down to the Moose Jaw area, across the Regina plains and down to the Souris at Weyburn, presents no formidable difficulties in these days of scientific engineering.
I have read that someone has suggested that any necessary pumping might be done by windmills; for the wind blows almost continually across the great plains. When I remember that windmills have been in operation for centuries in Holland, pumping water over dykes and out into the sea, I see no reason why equally cheap power should not be pumped from dammed rivers of western Canada over such heights of land as may be necessary to water at least a large part of these great plains. Electric power might be generated and utilized partly for this purpose. The valleys of both the Saskatchewan rivers lie between great banks and there are several places where dams could be conveniently located and power generated if desired. If it were necessary to divert some water from the North to the South Saskatchewan river, and to supplement the latter, irrigating the intervening county as it flowed, I believe that could be done.
Many people conceive of such channels being long straight cuts across the prairies, through hills and valleys; but that is not at all necessary. There are depressions running north and south and east and west which could form the basis for channels to be cut, and these could wind across the countryside following the line of least resistance and the most inexpensive engineering practice. The Kindersley, Rosetown and Biggar territories might be benefited in this way.
I have been told by engineers that dams placed at intervals on the South Saskatchewan, south of Saskatoon, to the point at which the Red Deer joins the South Saskatchewan in Alberta, would impound sufficient water to give moisture to the whole of central and south eastern Saskatchewan. I do not know. But that is something we should, as a parliament, find out. The little sloughs and large lakes now dry could be filled, and the table level of subsoil moisture raised again to its old level, while in many years an inch or two of water on the parched land at the rizht time would ensure a bountiful return for the labour expended.
Schemes like these should be investigated. I want to say quite frankly that as a layman I am not in a position to say whether such
schemes are feasible or not, and I therefore deprecate definite statements made by other laymen that irrigation is an impossibility in western Canada. I have heard persons who.
I am quite sure, know no more about this subject than I do, make the definite statement that all these schemes are quite impracticable. I am willing to admit that personally I do not know, but with the knowledge that I have I am persuaded that it is worth investigating. There are those who hold that a scheme of large-scale irrigation would involve an expenditure of $400,000,000. Personally that would not frighten me when I remember that we have spent more than $100,000,000 in recent years in agricultural relief, and have nothing to show for it, to say nothing of the enormous losses due to crop failures. But I am persuaded that for one-tenth of that $400,000,000 expenditure which some people have suggested would be necessary, lams could be built along the Smith Saskatchewan that would irrigate several million acres of good agricultural land. The larger scheme could, if necessary, be completed over a long period of years. When I see the puny efforts being made in western Canada, and contrast them with the great projects I have seen in the United States or read about in India or Africa, I realize that we should investigate thoroughly the possibilities of irrigation in our own country.
Last summer I went down into the United States and visited several of the great projects there. I went to the Fort Peck dam in the state of Montana, which is not, primarily, of course, an irrigation project but rather a flood control and power project, with irrigation as incidental to them both. There I saw an earth dam which will rise 240 feet above the river bed, the length of its main section across the river valley being
9.000	feet. The dam will contain approximately 105,000,000 cubic yards of earth,
1.600.000	cubic yards of rock, and 4,000,000 cubic yards of gravel. The great reservoir to be created by this dam across the Missouri river will store over 19,000,000 acre-feet of water. It will have a maximum surface area of 245,000 acres, and will be 180 miles long, with a maximum width of 16 miles. This will be one of the great new projects of North America. It will cost $100,000,000 and give employment to thousands of men who otherwise would be unemployed. Even the damming of either of the Saskatchewan rivers would be a relatively small affair compared to this.

speechtext:
How much land will it irrigate?
Drought Area-Mr. Coldwell

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext: I said that it is primarily not an irrigation project, but it will irrigate, as time goes by, large sections of a country which is much more difficult to irrigate than our prairie country. As the minister probably knows, it is situated in a hilly, semi-mountainous country, somewhat like our foothills, and the project is not primarily an irrigation project. It illustrates how vast quantities of water may be stored.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext: But there is plenty of prairie down below.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
Yes, and that would be irrigated. I saw the American projects around Malta, Montana, and drove from the arid prairie into a veritable garden of Eden, as did the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) just a few days before I arrived there. I then drove on across the mountains and saw another project in the state of Washington, where a desert looking very like our prairie will be watered by the Grande Coulee development from the Columbia river. There they are going to irrigate several millions of acres of desert country. These are giant undertakings, and from an examination of contour maps on both sides of the line I am convinced that irrigation projects on the great Canadian plains are relatively small when compared to these.
There are those who criticize such proposals on the ground of expense, but the alternatives are too terrible to face. Either we shall have to keep thousands of people on almost continuous relief or remove them from the lands they now occupy. Railways have been built to open up these territories and to serve communities established along the way. Men and women have built their homes there and unless we can rehabilitate this great area they face utter ruin. Schools and churches, with the usual business necessities, have been established and will have to be abandoned. The effect upon the economic structure of all Canada will eventually be profound, for eastern industry has as much interest in this rehabilitation as have the people who live there to-day. Rehabilitation of the country would not only rescue the people from poverty, misery and relief but would make available lands upon which thousands of our young people might establish homes, and might live, under proper conditions, in comparative security.
I am suggesting then that an investigation be made to see if any of these projects are feasible and that large scale irrigation if feasible should be undertaken as a national

plan and as a national responsibility. There are those, as I have said, who will lift their hands in horror at the proposed expenditures; some will call them handouts to the west. But in days gone by much larger handouts of these very lands were made by the federal government to powerful interests and corporations whose headquarters were located in our eastern cities. What a wonderful gift it was. The inalienable right in perpetuity to this land was given to corporations who, without regard to surface or soil analyses, turned them over to hardy pioneers whose efforts turned them into farms, but whose obligations caused them to deplete the rich reserves of moisture and chemicals that nature had stored through bygone years.
In recent years great irrigation schemes have been brought to successful conclusion in other parts of the British empire. British engineers have watered deserts in Africa and India; in the province of Sind in India the Lloyd barrage is one of the wonders of the world. When that scheme to utilize the river Indus is fully developed it will water 7,500,000 acres and bring security in a land where the desert has made life uncertain and caused suffering to many millions. Of the great projects in the Sudan and in northern Africa I do not propose to say anything at the moment, because I have not the time; but in North America, in India and in Africa, American and British engineers have, after careful surveys, watered the deserts there, giving economic security and crop certainty not only to those who till the soil, but to millions who depend on the products of that toil for their subsistence.
My resolution does not ask the government to undertake any such projects, but to obtain an authoritative survey in order that we may know whether such a scheme for western Canada is scientifically feasible and economically sound. My suggestion now is that such a committee should consist, not of departmental officials whose ideas have perhaps been moulded to some extent by the political environment in which they find themselves, but rather of authorities such as engineers who have been connected with one or other of the great projects to which I have alluded. If it were possible, an engineer in charge of the Indus development, an engineer who has had charge of the Sudan development, an American engineer connected with one of the great projects in the United States, and a Canadian engineer of outstanding ability in this direction, or any two or three of them, would make a commission whose authority and standing could not be questioned. My objection to what has been

Drought Area-Mr. Bothwell
said throughout the country regarding irrigation, both for and against, is that it is being said by laymen, men often filled perhaps with political prejudice and not equipped to give authoritative judgment upon matters of this description.
I have not dealt with the power which could be developed by large-scale irrigation schemes, but in my opinion that would electrify the whole of the Canadian northwest, bringing new comfort and power to the people who live there in this age of electricity. Moreover, in mixed farming areas, it would enable farmers to refrigerate their dairy and meat products and do much to improve the standards of Canadian farm produce on the markets of the world. For these and other reasons, which will no doubt be brought out by other speakers, I urge the adoption of the resolution.
I believe that the time has come when we have to consider this problem of the rehabilitation of western agriculture on a much larger scale than anything we have thought of doing up to the present time. I do not want to emphasize the misery and want and difficulties that face the people; I do not want to emphasize the hopelessness for the children who now live there, the difficulties in schools and the condition of teachers, all of which are due to the long periods of economic disaster and crop failure in that country. But I believe that we shall not be doing our duty if we simply say that these proposals are not feasible or if we say that the rain will fall again and the crops will grow. The history of the western country shows clearly that throughout the years that have gone by there have been from time to time long dry periods as well as wet ones, and if we have a wet period coming now we are sure it will be followed by a period without sufficient moisture. We must face that fact. I am not asking the house to authorize any particular irrigation scheme, but rather to obtain the very best advice that it is possible to get wherever we may find it, anywhere in the world, in order that we may know whether large scale irrigation is feasible or not.

speechtext:
I am sure the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) will pardon me if I do not specifically follow him in his remarks. I am quite in sympathy with the tone of the resolution, but I am afraid that before I get through the house will judge that I am not able to go quite as far as the hon. member did. Nor do I entirely follow some of the arguments he has made. It is perhaps fortunate that to-day this same subject is under
discussion in the legislature of Saskatchewan. On Thursday last a resolution was introduced by Mr. Stork to which an amendment was proposed by the provincial Minister of Public Works when the subject came up for discussion. The amendment rather appealed to me in the moderation of its terms. The amendment was:
That this assembly expresses its gratitude for the appropriations made by the federal government in its general rehabilitation program and for the works begun and constructed in Saskatchewan for the conservation and utilization of water for irrigation and stock watering purposes; and further
This assembly would respectfully request that sufficient moneys be provided from year to year so that detailed surveys of all watersheds not yet fully investigated be carried on with a view to facilitating the construction of all necessary projects found to be economically feasible, and also that the whole federal program be so extended and enlarged as to include the entire province.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext: Would the hon. member also read the motion?

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
The motion was as
follows:
That this assembly respectfully request the federal government to set aside an appropriation of at least $50,000,000 this year, to be used in investigation and completion of feasible water conservation, irrigation and other projects, directed towards the permanent rehabilitation of the drought area of this province.
This question of conservation of moisture in the prairie provinces and the rehabilitation of the farmers there perhaps goes back to the time mentioned by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. The Palliser report and reports of the early surveyors in the prairie regions did express doubts as to whether, on account of the lack of rainfall, the great central plains region would be suitable for agricultural purposes. Back in 1901, in the territory which is now comprised within the boundaries of Saskatchewan, we had only about 100,000 people. Since that time, through continued years of sufficient moisture to grow crops, the influx of settlers became very great, until at the present time we have 930,000 odd in that area of Saskatchewan. From the early settlement down to 1929 the people who settled there were able to make a good living. They found the soil productive, and they were able to build roads, bridges, schools, government and municipal buildings, and all that sort of thing; and the debt of the province up to 1929 was more than represented by physical assets in the province. Since 1929, on account of the drought, the country has not been the finest place in the world to

Drought Area-Mr. Bothwell

live in, and the debts of individuals, municipalities and governments have mounted up tremendously.
By 1934 the dominion government realized that the taking of steps to rehabilitate that area had become a federal responsibility, and an act was later passed by the federal government under the leadership of the present leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett) known as the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. Moneys were appropriated under that act and an organization set up to see what should be done to rehabilitate the area. That work has been carried on ever since, more money being expended each year, under three heads -reclamation, conservation and rehabilitation. We believe that the experience gained in the expenditure of that money has taught those who are interested in the projects on the ground, as well as people generally throughout the dominion, that the work that is being done is well worth while, and we all hope to see the complete rehabilitation of that whole area.
I might say in passing that I think the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act had the support of every hon. member in the house, no matter what his political affiliations. The intention was that some form of organization should be set up under which we would be able by some means to reclaim lands that were drifting and blowing away; also that we should find a way to conserve the rainfall and prevent its being carried off in spring freshets. Farmers or settlers in areas that have suffered severely from drought conditions and whom the organization could not see means of rehabilitating in the area in which they were located could be moved to other lands where they would have a chance of making good. In connection with the work of this rehabilitation board the first major step that had to be considered was what had been achieved in the past by the methods followed. In that connection I think I should go back to the work done through the dominion experimental farm at Indian Head many years ago. There they developed the idea of summer fallow for the purpose of conserving moisture. The next step in the rehabilitation plan was the development of marquis wheat, practically eliminating, as it did, the frost hazard in those areas and moving a considerable distance north the limit of territory upon which wheat could be grown. Marquis wheat has now become the standard of quality in hard spring wheats throughout the world.
The next step came in Alberta, by the introduction of strip farming and trash covering of the soil for the purpose of conserving

moisture. The objectives of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act may now be outlined as follows:
1.	Establishing of dominion experiment substations which are essentially outposts of the dominion experimental farms, set up under the rehabilitation program.
2.	Organizing of agricultural improvement associations where individual farmers and ranchers organize for community activity, including establishing of strip farming and trash cover crop methods to control soil drifting, regrassing work and tree planting.
3.	Reclamation stations established for the purpose of reclaiming land for agricultural use or of reestablishing a suitable grass cover on land which has been severely damaged by drought and soil drifting and has become a public menace.
4.	Grass development for the purpose of determining improved methods of establishing grass on land subject to soil drifting.
5.	Tree planting, including free distribution of trees and large scale demonstrations of field shelter belts.
6.	Establishing of a fully equipped soils laboratory at Swift Current experimental station for the purpose of continuing investigations of soil moisture and soil drifting in the drought area.
7.	Continuation of soil survey and soil classification in the drought area in cooperation with the provincial departments.
8.	Large scale soil moisture conservation projects, including contouring, terracing and furrowing to determine the value of such work.
9.	Agricultural economic survey throughout the drought area.
10.	Financial assistance in reestablishing settlers now on sub-marginal lands and reseeding of these lands for community pasture purposes.
11.	Assistance in developing a sheep and cattle policy in connection with sub-marginal lands developed for community pasture purposes.
12.	Engineering and financial assistance to individuals and communities in building dug-outs, stoekwatering dams and irrigation schemes where feasible.
These are the objectives of the prairie farm rehabilitation board, and for the past few years they have been working along these lines. It is quite true, as the hon. member who preceded me has said, no person who has not seen the drifting areas of western Canada can appreciate just what they are like. Last August I circled through a stretch of territory where scarcely a green thing of any description was to be seen; with soil drifting, rolling all the time, even though scarcely any wind was noticeable. The experimental farm at Swift Current, with the assistance and perhaps under the direction of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation board, experimented on about ten thousand acres of land scattered throughout that area in half sections. They used different methods in different places to find how they could control

Drought Area-Mr. Bolhwell
this soil drifting, and they believe they have found a method of doing so. There is a large area, however, that has to be looked after. It extends perhaps from some place east of Swift Current to about Bassano in Alberta, south to the United States border, and north of the South Saskatchewan river as far as Lloydminster. Throughout all that area work has been done with the assistance of the experimental farms. One day last August, when driving along there were times that I could scarcely see the radiator of the car. I had to creep along the side of the road in case some other car might come out of the dust storm. Finally I came to a half-section of land just south of the railway track at Fox Valley where work had been done with the help of the dominion experimental farm. I thought the storm had gone down, that it was all over, but after I got past that half section of land I found the situation just as bad as ever.
There they had listed the west side of the land with a new machine called a lister, which throws up a heavy furrow. They had run this lister one trip across the half section, north and south, every eight rods. They found that they were able to stop this drifting by doing that-not necessarily every eight rods but possibly every twenty rods, depending upon the type of soil in which they were working. In discussing the matter with the superintendent of the experimental farm at Swift Current I was informed-and I presume it will be in his report to the department- that the territory comprised within the area I mentioned will have to be farmed in a way somewhat similar to that I have indicated, by using a lister or some machine that will do similar work. A cultivator properly equipped may and will do just as satisfactory work, and in the trenches dug by these machines they are able to conserve whatever moisture there may be.
In addition they believe that by a system of terracing throughout that area, with machines such as I have described, they will be able to conserve a considerable portion of the normal run-off water in the spring and also the rain that falls during the storms, of which we have a few even in the driest part of the area. In addition, under the 'Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act they are encouraging farmers to put in dugouts, small irrigation projects and stock watering dams. According to my information, up to January 15 of this year over eleven thousand applications had been received from the three prairie provinces in connection with these small projects. Over half of this number, or over 7,100, were from Saskatchewan; 1,800 were from Manitoba and less than 2,500 were from Alberta. Over 820 of the applications received have been cancelled, rejected or dropped, leaving over 10,500 active applications, in addition to hundreds of letters that are receiving attention. Of these applications approximately 5,500 have been authorized or approved for construction, and of these nearly 4,300 have been completed or reported completed.
That is not going to solve the whole difficulty in that country, but the prairie farm rehabilitation board and the officials of the experimental farms have encouraged the farmers to form agricultural improvement associations in various parts of the province. To-day something over one hundred of those agricultural improvement associations have been formed. The object of that is to get the farmers who are interested in a particular district together so that they can discuss their difficulties and in unison work out some Dlan whereby not only the individual but also the whole community will be assisted. It is believed that more can be accomplished by getting the people on the land to work together to assist themselves than can be done by any widespread government expenditure of money.
In addition to the conservation of moisture in dams, dugouts and small irrigation projects, the terracing of land, the use of the lister and that sort of thing, they have worked out a scheme whereby the lands that are not properly arable will be taken out of cultivation. In the province of Saskatchewan we have, I think, about 30,000,000 acres of broken land. In 1936 there was something over
22.000.	000 acres actually seeded, and an area about one-third that size would be in summer fallow, which would bring the total to around
30.000.	000 acres. It is authoritatively stated that large scale irrigation projects in that province cannot take care of more than
1,500,000	acres.

speechtext:
My authority is the engineers in Regina who are interested in the work. It has been so stated by the chairman of the board and also by the Hon. Mr. Spence, who I believe is the liaison officer between the board and the federal government. Then, I have personally discussed the matter with engineers, particularly Mr. McGavin of the water rights branch in Regina, and Mr. Russell, chief engineer on the rehabilitation program. Although a complete survey of all possible projects has not yet been made, nevertheless

Drought Area-Mr. Bothwell
I believe these gentlemen are pretty well satisfied that large-scheme irrigation projects in Saskatchewan are not possible, because they estimate that the total amount of water obtainable there is only about 11,000,000 acre feet, and about a third of that will be lost in the process of irrigation.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
No, I am not able to answer the hon. member's question, without making a search. I have the information, though. Then, in Saskatchewan the condition is different from that in Alberta, due to the fact that the land to be irrigated is higher than the water which would be used in irrigation, and the water would accordingly have to be lifted, In Alberta there is the possibility of tapping streams without the necessity of an expensive system of dams, ^ and that water could be carried down to irrigate the lower lands.
While I am not opposed to irrigation projects, and while I believe that some projects are feasible-for instance, the one from River-hurst mentioned by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar-may I point out that, as I understand the term, and from the hon. member's description of the size of the Fort Peck dam, no large scale irrigation projects are contemplated. A project may be feasible around Herbert, and there may be the possibility of another one near Vanguard, within territory with which I am familiar.
Some of these irrigation projects may be feasible, and possibly should be constructed. But we are still not taking care of all the area. In addition to that, a considerable amount of land within the area should not be used for agricultural purposes-that is, should not be used for farming purposes. At the present time there is a plan to have areas which should not have been broken thrown back into community pastures in an endeavour to have such lands covered with grass and made them capable of producing crops for the sustenance of range stock.
Real success has been achieved along these lines in the experiments carried out at the Scott experimental station within the last four or five years. That station particularly has been experimenting with different kinds of grasses, and they find that the crested wheat grass is possibly a solution to the difficulty of getting those lands covered with grass and putting them in a condition where they can produce feed for stock which may run there.
I was much surprised to find the extent to which crested wheat grass may .be the salvation

of the province. Tests have been made in the past five years at the Scott station with respect to both cattle and sheep. In 1937 an attempt was made through the use of cattle to determine the relative amount of pasture obtained from grasses. The pasture fields compared were native pasture, brome, western rye and crested wheat grass. In this series the crested wheat grass was sown on the higher land to give it a more rigid test. The animals were rotated on the fields. The fields were fenced separately, and the pastures were not overgrazed. The native grass gave ten cow days per acre; western rye mixed with alfalfa gave forty; brome gave forty-nine, and crested wheat grass gave fifty-eight. To state this in another way, the relative amount of pasture from these fields was, with crested wheat grass equalling 100 per cent, brome 84 per cent, western rye with alfalfa 69 per cent, and native pasture 17 per cent.
In connection with sheep the difference in the third year was still greater. The statement is made that when western rye was practically all dead and gave no pasture, brome provided 38 per cent of the pasture and crested wheat grass gave 62 per cent. Averaging the three years, crested wheat grass provided about half the pasture on the three fields in question, brome provided slightly over one-third, and western rye provided approximately one-fifth.
These are the views of the superintendent of the dominion experimental station at Scott, Saskatchewan. In his statement he says that crested wheat grass must possess a powerful root system, and goes on to say:
After three years the sod from these grasses was ploughed. Western rye appeared not much better than a good grain stubble, brome looked much better, but crested wheat matched the best prairie sod.
Then, later on he says:
Another institution has collected information which further illustrates the comparative sod forming value of these three _ grasses. The pounds per acre of root fibre in the top six inches of soil from these grasses which had been down for three years was found to be 1,795 pounds for western rye grass, 3,783 for brome grass and 5,079 for crested wheat grass. Furthermore, excavation of these root systems showed western rye roots penetrated the soil to a depth of sixty-four inches, brome sixty-five inches and crested wheat grass ninety-six inches.
It is believed by the superintendent at the Scott station that crested wheat grass, together with the conservation of moisture through the methods I have briefly described, will save a great part of the affected area. Then, by the small irrigation projects many farmers can instal on their farms they will be able to

Drought Area-Mr. Quelch
grow from ten to twenty acres of alfalfa, which would tide them over in years of severe drought.
With these various methods it is believed that a continuation of the work now carried on under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act would be more than justified. No tremendous expenditure of money would be required, although we will have to spend more than has been spent in any previous year. Much of the initiatory work has been done, and if we are to rehabilitate the area these projects will have to be carried out.
To illustrate what has happened I obtained from the experimental farm photographs of areas on which they have worked. About forty miles south of Swift Current, near Cadillac, there was drifting soil to such a degree that most people believed recovery impossible. They did not think it could ever be put back into grass. If one were to see pictures of the drifting soil, of buildings half covered with silted soil, and sand a foot deep on the land, and then look at pictures of the same piece of land with a crop of spring rye growing on it in the spring of 1937, he would be amazed. I quote from the descriptive matter in connection with one of these pictures having to do with the Cadillac reclamation area:
Sufficient cover has been obtained to sow grass seed on the stubble. Rainfall during 1937 was practically nil. The methods practised enabled the growing of this crop.
Then there is a picture of a crop of spring rye which comes up to a man's knees. That was grown on a piece of land that had had a foot of moving silt on it. Down near Mort-lach there is another area where the same condition of drifting soil existed. This area has been recovered. One field had been abandoned and had nothing but Russian thistle, tumbling mustard and prairie sage growing on it. A picture is shown of a stand of crested wheat grass on the same field. The caption under the photograph reads:
Seed was drilled in among the weed cover without any cultivation in April, 1936. Seedlings same up in spring of 1936 but appeared to die off during the hot, dry summer that followed. In 1937 the plants revived, made a good growth and produced seed.
These are actual photographs taken on the ground, and they show just what can be done. These experiments were carried on by the experimental farm under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and they have demonstrated clearly just what is possible in the way of recovery and reclamation. The conservation of moisture by methods found feasible up to the present time, the saving of all run-off
water in the spring instead of allowing it to run away as it has been doing, proper methods of cultivation in order to stop drifting, the establishment of stock watering dams and small irrigation projects, and the taking out of cultivation of the lighter soils which, as is now known, should never have been broken up, have all been demonstrated. We believe that with a continuation of the work that has been done under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act and with possibly a greater expenditure of money from year .to year than has been expended in the past, we shall be able to save all of the area referred to by the previous speaker, and which I have described as extending throughout a tremendous part of that prairie country. Later on in the session, when the estimates are being considered, I hope we will have an opportunity of considering the extension of this program which has been found so feasible for the west.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, generally speaking I find myself in agreement with the objects of this motion and therefore I shall support it. I would direct attention to the fact that the federal government have incurred a certain amount of responsibility for the conditions that exist to-day in the drought areas, because they were in charge of the natural resources of these provinces when the lands were thrown open for settlement in spite of warnings issued by prominent engineers and government surveyors that they were too dry for settlement. To-day we are reaping the tragic consequences of the policy carried out at that time. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) has covered thoroughly this particular aspect of the matter, and I shall not take up the time of the house to go over the ground again.
Last fall I received a number of articles from England written by Mr. A. G. Street, a farmer journalist who some twenty years ago had resided for three years in Manitoba. Last summer he returned to Canada and made a tour of the west. He has been criticized severely for the gloomy and tragic picture he paints of the drought area, but, in my opinion it is no more gloomy or tragic than the actual conditions that exist in many parts of this area. Mr. Street referred to the methods of farming which had been followed in these areas in past years, and his comments in this connection have also been criticized. While I realize that some of his arguments may not have been well founded, as a farmer who has resided for some thirty years on the edge of the drought area I know that our methods have been at fault. This fact was
Drought Area-Mr. Quelch

Prior to 1921 there was a good deal of interest in and discussion of a large-scale irrigation project, and in 1922 a preliminary survey was made of what is called the North Saskatchewan project. It is generally known as the William Pearce project. The proposal was to divert water from the North Saskatchewan to the Clearwater and the Red Deer rivers, then take it down to Sullivan lake, where a storage reservoir of some million-acre feet would be formed; then carry it by the Eyehill creek and Sounding creek into Tramping lake in Saskatchewan. Below Sullivan lake approximately 470,000 acres would be irrigated and one million acres in Saskatchewan. Under the total project about
1.500.000	acres would have been irrigated and the total cost would have been 8105,000,000. The cost, however, of carrying water from Sullivan lake to Tramping lake would have been excessive owing to the very sandy nature of the soil through which the water would have to be carried. It would have run the cost to about $70 an acre to irrigate the land in Saskatchewan, and for that reason the scheme has been generally condemned. On the other hand there is for Alberta a modified scheme known as the Sullivan lake project, which is believed to be thoroughly sound. Under this project the water would be diverted from Clearwater river and carried down Stauffer creek into the Red Deer river; then a dam fifty feet high would be placed below the mouth of Raven river and the water would be carried, by a canal 146 miles long, to Sullivan lake where 437,000 acres would be irrigated.

This is a survey that was made by the engineering department and it has been declared absolutely sound. The article is about five pages long and gives a complete description of the engineering features and the sizes of the various reservoirs. I shall be glad to pass it on to the hon. gentleman and he will get full information from it. It is a matter of engineering technique which I should not care to go into now. The areas irrigated below Sullivan lake would be 73,190 acres between Sullivan lake and Hanna; in the Berry creek area, 304,930 acres, and in the Monitor area, 49,240 acres. The total cost would be approximately $23,000,000. In addition to that, another
142.000	acres could be irrigated on the west side of the Red Deer river along Ghost Pine,

Knee Hill and Three Hills, bringing the total cost to $27,000,000; and the total amount irrigated would be 580,000 acres.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), speaking in Alberta, said that the Sullivan lake project would cost $28,000,000; but at the time he must have been confusing the two projects, because according to the reclamation surveys-and that is the only record there is-the cost of the Sullivan lake project only would be $23,000,000 while the Sullivan lake project, plus the irrigation scheme on the west side of the Red Deer, would be $27,000,000.
I have discussed this project with the officials of the Department of Agriculture in Alberta, and they say that it is desirable. I have discussed it with the head of the water resources department, Mr. Charlesworth, and he tells me that from the engineering point of view the scheme is absolutely sound. That being so, what would appear to be the main objections? Well, once again we seem to have the same old bugbear; we have arrived at the same dead end that we have reached whenever we have discussed anything else of a progressive nature-the question of money: Where is the money to come from to finance a scheme of this kind?
We must remember that the existence of the drought area is not a local responsibility; it is recognized to-day as a national problem and a national responsibility, and as such it might well be financed under the proclaimed Liberal policy of currency and credit in terms of public need. The project should be carried out as a national responsibility without placing a capital charge against the irrigated land. If we were to try to recover the total cost of such a project by making it a charge against the land it would be absolutely impossible for the farmer to make a living and at the same time pay that charge, and no doubt that is the reason why many irrigation projects in the province have had their difficulties. They have failed owing to the high capitalization of the schemes.
This project is especially desirable in view of the fact that practically all the land which would be irrigated is already owned by the government under the special areas board, and therefore they would be in a position to divide the land into small economic units so that the farmer would have enough irrigated land to make it possible for him to grow feed and seed and to sustain his family.
I would imagine that in Saskatchewan it would be possible to put in similar projects in the area that might be classified as a permanent drought area, and we in this comer

Drought Area-Mr. Donnelly
shall be only too glad to support the motion in the hope that this government may find ways and means of carrying out progressive measures of the kind I have described.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
I find myself in accord with much that has been said this afternoon regarding the condition of the people in the dried out area of western Canada. I have listened with a great deal of interest to the discussion of the drought in western Canada and what can be done to bring about an improvement in conditions there.
The present state of affairs in western Canada is serious; it is one of the biggest problems facing the dominion to-day. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) last year told us that the dried out area in the west represented one-fourth of all the land occupied in Canada, and one-fifth of all improved farm land in Canada. In other words the drought area covers about 18,000,000 acres of improved land and 35,000,000 acres of occupied land in western Canada. It is important to the lives of about one million people in Canada. In my opinion it is a greater problem than even the railway problem. The question what we are to do with this great drought area we have in western Canada is the big problem we have to solve.
In 1934 in the house I advised the then Conservative government to make a survey of drought conditions in that part of the country and to determine for themselves what they would do. One of two conclusions could be reached, either that it was possible to farm this land, or that it was not possible to do so. If it is not possible to farm the land then it is necessary to help the people to move out, and if it is possible for the people to live in that part of the country and to farm it, then they should be given instructions in the proper methods of farming that land, and shown how to cultivate the land so as to make a living in that district. That seemed to be the conclusion. Shortly after that the Conservative government put through a rehabilitation act and work was begun towards a survey of this country in an endeavour to rehabilitate some of our people there. I agree with much that has been said with regard to the condition in that part of the country, but I do not agree with the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) when he tells us what the cause of the condition there is.
