subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
I have been farming for more than thirty years and I think I know something about agriculture. If you tell me that when you cultivate the land you prevent the water from soaking into it, that the water runs off, and that it soaks better into sod land than into cultivated land, then I must find serious fault with such a theory. I cannot agree with it at all. Any man who has farmed knows that after a rainfall, when you go and look at the sod you may find the water has soaked two or three inches into it, whereas if you cross the road and look at the cultivated land you will find that the water has soaked down eight or ten inches. That is the reason why our sloughs and dams and reservoirs have dried up; the water has soaked down into the cultivated land and has not been running off as it did when the sod was there. There is no doubt of that. We have been farming in order to conserve moisture, to allow the moisture to go down into the land and stay there as subsoil moisture. That is the object of summer fallow, deep ploughing. I disagree with the statement that the condition there was caused by cultivating the land and letting the water run away.
Since this rehabilitation act was passed the purpose has been to teach the farmers, to show them how they may ensure a crop in the dried out area, how they may seed their land and farm it in such a way that even in the drought area they may be assured of some crop, some return for their efforts. With this object one of the first things the government did in Saskatchewan was to make a soil survey. It was absolutely necessary to know what the land was. In the early days when the land was first taken up the price of wheat was good and people were anxious to get land; the land was offered free and people rushed in and took up any land they found available with the idea of cropping it for a few years, getting a few good crops and then perhaps getting out. Much land was taken up and farmed which never should have been taken, sub-marginal land. Now we find much of that land has been abandoned. This soil survey has been completed in Saskatchewan and at present an economic or agricultural survey is being made to discover the condition of the different farmers. That is being done in order to find out what should be done in the different districts. This survey has already been completed in some of the worst districts, but the whole province has not yet been covered. On a lot of this sub-marginal land the taxes have not been paid; the land has gone back to the municipalities and they
Drought Area-Mr. Donnelly

have turned it over to the provincial government and the provincial government in turn to the federal government. They are fencing that land and, as the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) said, trying to get it into grass again. In Saskatchewan at present a great deal of land has been fenced and about twelve pasture areas, amounting to about 225,000 acres have been established. In Alberta some 595,000 acres have been fenced and pastured. Some buildings have also been built, dugouts, dams, reservoirs and corrals constructed, and up to date methods of cultivation adopted to produce proper pasture, with the idea of creating community pastures where the people, with the direction and assistance of the government, can raise better stock. We are helping the people to stock these pastures with better stock. This ia being done both in Saskatchewan and in Alberta. Besides that, I understand it is the intention of the government to set aside a certain amount of these pastures as reserves, so that in dry years it will not be necessary to ship a lot of cattle out to Manitoba and districts in northern Saskatchewan, but it will be possible to keep them right there in these pastures which have not been pastured down. These are some of the things that are being done with these sub-marginal lands.
Then we come to soil drifting. For years most of us did not know what soil drifting was. I have been farming in western Canada for some thirty years, and for probably twenty-five years of that time we did not know what soil drifting meant. It is only in the last few dry years that it has become a problem. I believe that when we have rain again, as we hope we shall in the near future, we shall not be troubled with soil drifting. In order to combat and prevent soil drifting certain steps have been taken. One method is strip farming. If your farm is, say, half a mile long, you cultivate strips twelve to fifteen rods wide and put in a crop; on the next twelve to fifteen rods you will not have any crop but will let it stay in stubble, and so on alternately. This will prevent the soil from drifting. There is no doubt this has a certain beneficial effect. If you have a whole section in summer fallow, once it begins to drift at one end the drifting will spread over the whole field.
Besides strip farming we also sow grass seed in order to get back to grass. To help in this the government have started experimental substations, to the number of something like forty-seven, demonstrating the way to farm in order to prevent drifting. Also we have organized throughout western Canada what are known as agricultural improvement

associations, of which we have some eighty-five. In these associations the people meet together to talk over their difficulties; they agree to follow the directions of the men from the experimental farms and substations as to the best way to farm the land. Also men from these substations are going out and sowing grass seed on the rough land, and broadcasting or sowing it with seeders on prepared land. They are sowing it with and without cover crops, with the idea of determining which is the best way to get the land back into grass. So far they are not sure which is the better way, but they make certain recommendations. The membership in these agricultural improvement associations numbers about 11,000 or 12,000 farmers, and to these farmers a certain amount of grass seed is given free for experimental work. During 1935-36 the government gave out, of crested wheat grass, something like 86,000 pounds; brome grass, 25,000 pounds; western rye grass,
8,000	pounds; sweet clover, 35,000 pounds; alfalfa, 7,000 pounds; alsike clover, 500 pounds; timothy, 1,000 pounds; reed canary grass, 500 pounds; cereal grains, 386,000 pounds, making in all 550,000 pounds of grass seed that they have given out freely to these people to sow.
In addition, certain areas have been taken over entirely by the substations in order to try to bring them back under cultivation. This is done where land has started to drift, continues to drift and has been forsaken and is drifting over good land in the immediate neighbourhood. Last year I had an opportunity of going out and seeing several of these areas and watching the work done, and I feel sure that much of this land will be brought back again in the near future and sown to grass.
Another thing being done relates to trees. Some of our theorists claim that trees bring rain, other people say that rain brings trees. Where we have trees we have rain, they say; others say that where you have rain you have trees. In the United States they are experimenting with tree planting. They are planting trees in rows six rods wide every mile for one hundred miles; that will be, as it were, one hundred patches six rods wide and a mile apart, extending from the Canadian boundary to the gulf of Mexico. I do not know if that will determine the question whether or not trees bring moisture; it is hard to say what will be the result over an area of that size; but if these trees grow, in the next forty or fifty years some of the people living then will be able to come to some conclusion on that point. I have often thought that if we on the plains had moisture we would have

Drought Area-Mr. Donnelly
trees; that it is the moisture which brings the trees and not the trees which bring the moisture.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
Where we have more
moisture in the west we have more trees.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
That is so. But there is just this I want to say with regard to that matter. Under our tree planting policy in the past, especially on the bald prairies, the short grass country, we have tried to concentrate on putting trees around a man's house. That may be a laudable idea but it has many faults. The place where the trees should be planted is the lowest land belonging to a farm. Invariably a man builds his house on the highest piece of land he has. Then, when he plants trees around his house he plants them on the highest piece of land he has. I believe that is the worst place to grow trees. In the late winter or early spring, as soon as the warm weather begins, you have a chinook; the snow melts; the roots of the trees are more or less exposed, and the sap goes up the trees. Probably the next day a frost comes along and the trees are split open and killed. On the other hand if the trees were planted at the lowest point on a man's farm they would gather snow around them; it would not melt off so quickly; the trees would not be subject to chinooks and to having the sap rise too soon, and then they would not be frost killed, as they have been in the past.
I also believe that we have been getting the wrong kind of trees. We do not want trees with roots which spread out on the ground; we want trees which have tap roots, so that the sap will not rise so soon, and they will not be winter killed as they have been in the past. I am not referring to the park section. I know there you can plant poplars, Manitoba maples and so on, and do well with them. I am referring to the dried out area, the bald prairie. In that section of the country we want trees with tap roots, and we want to concentrate on planting those trees at the lowest points of the farms, in order that enough snow may be collected to furnish sufficient moisture to produce a garden, thus enabling a man to raise his own vegetables more than has been the case in the past.
I want to refer more particularly to water conservation and matters of that kind, rather than to trees. The water we have to conserve, or the water we have in the province of Saskatchewan, is from three principal sources. First, we have the ground water, which comes to us by means of springs or wells. On the farm we may have a spring, an artesian well. We have some shallow wells
and we also have some deep wells which go down 125, 200 or 250 feet. In some districts there is some irrigation by means of ground water, but not a very great deal. The next source is our rivers, or water that comes from the mountains, and in the latter case the water is almost continuous. We have our rivers, the South Saskatchewan, the North Saskatchewan and so on. Last of all, we have what we call our surface water, the run-off from the snow or rain, and in many districts that is the only moisture we have. That is practically the case in the district I represent.
With regard to my constituency I may say that practically speaking nine-tenths of the run-off goes into natural reservoirs, while the remaining one-tenth goes across the line into the United States. For example, we have Johnstone lake, Twelve Mile lake, Lake of the Rivers, Fife lake, Willow Bunch lake and others. These lakes have no outlets, or at least their outlets have not been in operation for the last twenty-five years. For all that, however, at the present time these lakes are absolutely dry. Where is our water for irrigation to come from? If you are going to have irrigation the first thing you must have is water. Where are you going to get that water? I have gone about from place to place in my constituency and told the people, "If you can show me any place where we can put in a dam I shall have an engineer come and look it over." Last year and the year before I travelled for about a month and a half, inspecting these various dams and reservoirs in Saskatchewan, and I know whereof I speak. We have had engineers in there to inspect these different locations, but our water is so slow in flowing and our channels are so deep that it is impossible to get the water out of them in order to do any irrigating. If you are going to do any at all, it is a pumping proposition. You must have pumps in order to get the water up so that you may use it.
As far as the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar is concerned, I welcome an investigation into this matter if it will do anything to help us irrigate our farms and be assured of crops, but in connection with many places in that area I do not know how it is going to help in any shape or form. We have, however, small dugouts, small dams and small irrigation projects. These are small works, but so far as I am concerned in western Canada these are really the big things. These small things are what we should concentrate on, because in my opinion if Saskatchewan is depending for its future upon the land it is going to irrigate, then that province is just about through. We are expecting moisture
Drought Area-Mr. Donnelly

and better farming conditions to return. Small dams, small reservoirs and dugouts will be of some advantage to the people living on the farms when the moisture returns and when, as in the past, we have a reasonable amount of rain. But if we get rain, as we hope to in the future, and as we have had it in the past, our irrigation projects will not be of much use to us, although at the present time we may think they would be.
It has always been found, in every country, that when there are trying conditions the people yell for irrigation. All of them want irrigation. But the moment the dry time passes and moisture returns they forget about the irrigation project; the country must look after that project and keep it in shape. I am satisfied that the government should go slowly in the matter. Do not rush into it and spend a lot of money. Do not say, "We will spend millions; we will have it all fixed up. Our people will then be all right." We know it will not be so. I do not believe that would be the result.
One hon. member referred to a project in the United States. In the states bordering on western Canada I believe there are thirty-one of those projects, and they cost about $193,000,000.

They have cut off a certain amount from year to year; they have now reached the point where they find that the people are not able to pay, and there is a grave doubt whether they will ever pay. It has been found that the settlers could not establish themselves and also meet the payment charges.
The projects in the United States involved a long and difficult task. People over there say that not only is it a long and difficult task, but they add that it is a very hard matter to take a man from dry farming, place him on irrigated land and teach him how to irrigate it. It is said that the man who is brought from the dry farm to the irrigated farm is more liable to pray for rain than to pay for irrigation. That has been the experience across the boundary line in connection with some of their projects.
Reference has been made to the Fort Peck dam. That was a wonderful undertaking w'hich took place just across the line from my constituency. That undertaking cost about $250,000,000.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
The engineers from the Fort Peck dam who come into our district all agree that in Canada we are going along the right line. They advise against large developments or extensive irrigation projects. We have moved slowly in these matters, and in future it may be necessary for us to continue that procedure. They advise us to go slowly in matters of this kind.
I would hope that in the future we shall have rain and shall not have to irrigate. With respect to the small dugouts, dams and small irrigation projects, may I say that at present we have an officer known as the agricultural supervisor. A man may send in his application to build a dam or dugout, and the supervisor will drive around to see

Drought Area-Mr. Donnelly
the location of the farm. If a dugout has been suggested the supervisor will advise the farmer that the dugout should be about 150 feet long, about sixty feet wide and at least ten feet deep. The officer marks out the planned work, and in turn the farmer goes ahead and does the digging. When he has dug it out, and the drainage from half a section, a section or two sections runs into it, it will probably be filled with water, and he will have a supply sufficient for his stock and his household requirements. He finds this a great help in watering his stock, and in the general care of his farm. If the water is about ten feet deep it will last throughout the year, and he is assured of a good water supply.
I have seen some of these dugouts which have been built by communities. These have been about 250 feet long, about 150 feet wide and about fifteen to twenty feet deep, and are projects well worth while. The government began by paying these people about three cents, and raised the rate to four and a half cents a yard. Last year the rate was raised to eight cents a yard. The farmer, with the use of his horses, cannot work for less than twelve cents a yard, so it would appear that he does not get paid for all his work. If the work is done with a drag-line or done by machinery, the farmer may be able to do the work for eight cents a yard. He may be able to get by at that rate. Then, as soon as the farmer has the dugout he must put a fence around it and must plant trees, in order to draw moisture and to hold the snow, so that the dam, dugout or reservoir may be filled.
Then, there are dams. In connection with these the agricultural expert comes along, looks the ground over and gives his decision. In addition, in Saskatchewan there is an engineer checking on the water rights. A survey is made, and the farmer is advised to go ahead. In turn the farmer proceeds to put in the dam, and ripraps it with stone. He gets a certain price for his stone, and a certain price for constructing the dam. The dam is beneficial in the same way. In many cases, with a small dam the farmer is able to irrigate half an acre, an acre or two or three acres and to raise some alfalfa and garden products. These dams are of great benefit to the people in the dried out areas. There are thousands of these dams; more and more people are building them. The people in western Canada are getting dam conscious.

We believe these dams would be a great help in carrying them through dry seasons. There are also stock watering
dams to be used by communities. For stock watering dams in large communities grants as high as $250 are allowed, and eight cents a yard paid. Two, three or four neighbours can go in together to build these and they may also obtain the assistance of the municipality.
In western Canada there are something like twenty larger projects being considered, all of which have to a certain extent to do with irrigation. For example, the ones at Val Marie, Coderre and Eastend are mainly for irrigation purposes. The main object of most of these irrigation projects is to provide forty or fifty acres to each farmer for grass or alfalfa. The pastures for stock will be up on the high lands and it is expected that in the dry years they will be able to raise enough feed and fodder for their stock.
I should like to give some of the reasons why certain of the larger projects have not been continued. I have before me a collection of the opinions of certain experts with regard to these matters. One man has suggested the possibility of irrigating from the Saskatchewan river. That may be possible, but I should like to quote what Mr. Charlesworth, one of the engineers, has to say. I quote:
The time may come when the construction of more of these larger projects may be desirable but for the present, however, with experience to date, it would seem doubtful whether the expenditure of a large amount of public funds would be wise and certainly not before some assurance was forthcoming that markets for irrigated products are available.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the burden of the resolution before the house for consideration at the moment touches particularly a part of this dominion and some hon. members may feel that a matter of this kind is peculiarly sectional and therefore to be discussed only by those who come from that part of the country affected. So far those who have spoken have come from western Canada, that part of the dominion which has been primarily affected by the conditions which inspire the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell). On the other hand, I feel it is important in connection with a matter which touches a section of the country as vitally as does this touch western Canada, that every hon. member should place on record his full recognition of responsibility. There is no section of Canada which is not a part of Canada. We are here as Canadians and, perforce, if we discharge our duties as we should, we should take a keen interest in those matters which may directly affect only a part of the country but which indirectly affect all parts.
As one who lives in Ontario I rise to speak on this resolution, not in specific terms or with any idea of discussing irrigation but in an attempt to convey to the house the fact that, after all, there are those of us who live in the eastern part of Canada who are vitally concerned with western Canada. For western Canada is as much a part of us as is our own province. One has heard it said repeatedly by those who come from the west that the east understands little about the west. Those of us who live in the east have heard it said altogether too often that we do not understand very much about the west and perhaps do not take enough interest in that part of our country. When such a great section of this dominion faces the problem which Saskatchewan faces at this time, it is incumbent upon us to give to that problem our best as Canadians. Our fellow Canadians are being impinged by circumstances at the moment beyond their control.
In the eighteenth century there lived a great American philosopher who was also a statesman and an erudite gentleman. I refer to Benjamin Franklin, of whom the fourteenth edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica has this to say:
Other men may have been greater, but very few have been more human.

He left for us many philosophical gems in which to delight, but perhaps no statement of his is more sententious than this aphorism:
We must all hang together, or assuredly we shall all bang separately.
There has been no sentence uttered in recent years that sounds a graver warning to us in Canada than do those words given to the world by Benjamin Franklin 160 years ago.
I am a firm believer in the rights of groups, whether they be minorities or majorities. I have the deepest and utmost respect for all considered opinions of men, and I firmly believe, as did the fathers of confederation, that local institutions and local laws of all the various provinces should be guaranteed. I am not parochial in outlook or narrow in viewpoint, and whereas I reside in one province I respect the rights of all provinces, just as I respect as a Canadian the rights of all the other dominions and the colonies of the British Commonwealth of Nations. I am not intolerant, and I dislike intensely bigotry and prejudice. I have at the same time a high regard for broad-mindedness and openmindedness. In other words, I am a firm believer in the spirit that motivated and made possible the Dominion of Canada. I am, you see, Mr. Speaker, a thorough Canadian in spirit as well as in name.
What has it meant and what does it mean to "hang together" in Canada? On Monday, February 6, 1865, the then attorney general, Sir John A. Macdonald, moved in the House of Commons a resolution which reads as follows:
That an humble address be presented to Her Majesty, praying that she may be graciously pleased to cause a measure to be submitted to the imperial parliament, for the purpose of uniting the colonies of Canada, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Prince Edward Island, in one government, with provisions based on certain resolutions which were adopted at a conference of delegates from the said colonies, held at the city of Quebec, on October 10, 1864.
As an ultimate result of this resolution the Dominion of Canada was born on July 1, 1867. Subsequently, what are now the provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia, became part of the dominion, so that to-day there is in the northern part of the north American continent a great British dominion stretching from the Atlantic to the Pacific, from the 49th parallel of latitude to the wastes of the arctic.
We are indeed a vast country geographically, though a small country numerically. Our population is concentrated in what is essentially a long, narrow strip of territory,

Drought Area-Mr. Massey
extending from coast to coast, along an international border across which lies one of the great nations of the world. We are British, and throughout Canada proclaim our allegiance, along with hundreds of millions of others throughout the world, to the one who is the quick and living centre of the spirit of empire, the personification of the nobility and tradition that belong to those who call themselves British, and we unitedly honour the crown.
We are a complex nation, not homogeneous in any sense of the word. Native within our borders are those of two great races, and we speak two languages.
We have also absorbed into our midst those who have come to our shores from all over Europe and from other continents as well, new Canadians, who in the main have adopted well and sincerely the customs, manners and modes of Canada. We are engaged in a wide diversity of activities. We are farmers, fishermen, miners, lumbermen, mechanics, and we practise all the trades. We have customs which vary widely across our dominion, stretching as it does across a whole continent, 3,500 miles in width.
The habitant of Quebec and the farmer of Ontario are as different in character and characteristics as the Devonshire yeoman and the Highland Scot. The ranchman in the west and the dairyman in the east have personalities as unlike as their occupations. Even the fisherman of British Columbia is a different sort of fellow from the fisherman of the maritimes, while the professional men of the eastern cities are in many ways unlike the professional men in the western cities. But in spite of all our differences in race, in customs, in religion, in habits and in personal and individual characteristics, in spite of the sectional divisions into which this country may so readily be divided, we are a Dominion of Canada, bom in 1867, and we have grown rapidly through the last seventy years to our present position of importance as a nation of the world.
Our growth has been as romantic as it has been steady, a growth possible only as a result of the fact that through those seventy years we have all "hung together."
As we look back through the years to 1867 we come to the instrument which was designed to give to us to-day the dominion in which we live-the British North America Act. Here was an act designed and brought into being by men of all shades of political opinion, an act in the designing and passing of which such notorious political enemies as George Brown and Sir John A. Macdonald joined forces, and hand in hand hurdled what seemed at first to be almost insuperable difficulties on the way to their common goal.
In their efforts they were supported fully, whole-heartedly and sincerely by many eminent Canadians, prominent among whom was Sir George Etienne Cartier. Have we justified the faith reposed in us by the fathers of confederation? As Canadians we may well be proud in many ways of the accomplishments of this nation. Under the handicap of g1 eat space, under the difficulties of extremes of climate, under the hazards and hardships that beset the path of the pioneer, under the menace of possible incipient and unconscious domination by a mighty nation to the south of us, we have progressed to our present degree of national importance and to the point where we are held in international respect. To-day we are eleven millions of people, actively engaged in agriculture, industry and commerce. At first, in our earlier days, we were an agrarian country, bending our full efforts toward the development of our agriculture and agricultural products. In this century we have added the pursuits of industry and commerce, until to-day we are fifth among the trading nations of the world. Not only are our agricultural and manufactured products widely accepted everywhere, but we are now one of the most important factors in both precious and base metals in the world's metal market.
I have taken the time of the house this afternoon, Mr. Speaker-and the house has listened most patiently-to discuss what I have discussed because it seems to me, as I said at the beginning of my remarks,' it is incumbent upon all hon. members, so important is the resolution introduced by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, to bend our full and united efforts towards finding a solution for this problem. We are challenged by what has been presented in this chamber to-day to realize anew that we are not east and west or nine separate and independent provinces, to forget our sectional differences, to attempt to overcome misunderstandings' and to make a combined and united effort towards the development of a Dominion of Canada that shall be a dominion in fact as well as in name.

speechtext:
When the house rose at six o'clock we were debating the resolution of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) with reference to rehabilitation of the drought area. I wish to continue for a short time the discussion of that resolution.

Drought Area-Mr. Evans
Coming from the southwest corner of Saskatchewan, from a constituency which has suffered severely from drought at different periods over the past thirty years, I believe that we who live in that southwest part and in the drought area have first hand knowledge of the difficulties and problems experienced by our settlers who settled in that district during the early part of the present century. I wish to speak particularly of the southwest portion of the province and to discuss the way in which the farm rehabilitation act applies to us in that district.
Our part of the province is in the plains area about which we have heard so much and we are peculiarly situated there owing to the fact that we are in a semi-arid district. We find that in our district and in the southeast corner of Alberta the situation is particularly adapted to the development of irrigation projects. Our part of the province was settled from about 1907 to about 1914 and in 1910 we had a severe drought in that area. Again in 1914 there was a very severe drought and a total crop failure.
The dominion government of that day, recognizing the severity of the drought of 1914, came to the assistance of the settlers in that area, particularly in southwestern Saskatchewan and southeastern Alberta, and furnished them with food, fuel, seed grain, and feed and fodder for their live stock. I bring this to the attention of the house for the reason that our district was then in the early stages of settlement, and the governments of that period should have realized that it was unsuited for the growing of cereals and the development of agriculture along that line. Prior to 1910 there had settled in that district many people who came in during the 90's-people who had developed the live stock industry-and when the government of Canada decided upon settlement in that area we destroyed the best ranching country in the world, with the result that we have developed a country which is not adapted to either farming or ranching.
We believe that the responsibility for conditions which now prevail in southwestern Saskatchewan rests at the door of this parliament. As late as 1918 we had petitions signed by settlers throughout the southwest asking the Department of the Interior at Ottawa to cancel leases and open up lease land for settlement. To-day the people who settled on these lands are not able to carry on because they settled on sub-marginal lands that were not fit for cultvation. This brings us to the present climax. We have come

through seven years of drought in southwestern Saskatchewan. We are trying to overcome in two or three years what has developed during the past thirty years, which is an impossibility. Many of our people are impatient because of the slow movement of the government in the endeavour to overcome conditions that have developed over thirty years.
As I have said, the southwest part of Saskatchewan and the southeast part of Alberta are adapted to irrigation, for these reasons. Down through the centre of the plains area there is a row of hills known as the Cypress hills, which are partly wooded. These hills are dotted here and there with small lakes and numerous springs which are sources of many streams. The streams running on the north and south slopes of the Cypress hills can easily be developed to irrigate land in small or large quantities as the case may be, but we have an opportunity to irrigate land only in the river valleys. There have been developed over past years in southwestern Saskatchewan many small irrigation projects, some of them dating back to 1892. These projects were developed at that early date on Maple creek, Bear creek and Battle creek, and are still in operation. Many tons of fodder have been cut off the lands irrigated by these private projects.
Since 1935, when the rehabilitation program came into force, there has been developed in southwestern Saskatchewan an irrigation scheme. To-day the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) referred to some of these projects. We find that the irrigation projects are being developed in Saskatchewan as rapidly as possible, and while the rehabilitation program is in its third year it is still to some extent in the formative stage and new measures are being undertaken as conditions warrant. The water development program is progressing more rapidly and we are establishing reservoirs of surplus water for stock watering and irrigation purposes. In many districts we are developing large irrigation projects. Take, for instance, the development of the Frenchman river. This river takes almost the entire run-off on the south slope of the Cypress hills. There have been developed so far- in the Frenchman river valley an irrigation project at Yal Marie and one at Eastend. Last year the Yal Marie project had under cultivation about 1,200 acres, and from some of this land there was produced thirty bushels of No. 1 wheat to the acre. On the rest of it we grew fodder and some garden truck. The Eastend project had some crop on it -last year, but it is not quite

Drought Area-Mr. Evans
as well developed as Val Marie. This year we have ready for cultivation on the Val Marie project some 4,000 acres.
The Val Marie and Eastend projects have to be supported by a fresh reservoir that is being developed at Cypress lake, which is the head of Frenchman river. This project is now under development, and when fully developed it will irrigate between 30,000 and
40,000	acres along the Frenchman river valley. We know from experience, from the crops grown and the development at Val Marie; that the soil and climatic conditions are suitable for irrigation farming, and all we need is the full development of the water supply. Further development at Eastend will enable us to irrigate between 6,000 and 7,000 acres. When the Cypress lake reservoir is fully developed it will also furnish additional water to continue irrigation in the Battle creek area of another 6,000 to 8,000 acres of land. In addition to the development of this south run-off of the Cypress hills we have under development the Downey lake project. This is on the north slope of the Cypress hills, and is located about twelve miles southwest of Maple creek. This project when completed, and supplemented by other smaller creeks and dams, will make it possible to irrigate another 6,000 to 8,000 acres along the Maple creek valley and its tributaries. Many other creeks on the north run-off of the Cypress hills are being surveyed and we expect will be developed during the coming summer.
One other outstanding development for which engineers have completed their surveys and supplemented their report is located about forty miles southeast of Swift Current, near the town of Vanguard, and is known as the Vanguard project. This when fully developed has the possibility of irrigating between 15,000 and 16,000 acres of some of the best land in Saskatchewan. We expect that this project may be developed this coming season. The development of this project will solve the feed problem of a large portion of southern and central Saskatchewan. Irrigation goes hand in hand with live stock, so we have in southwestern Saskatchewan the development of irrigation projects to supply winter feed for our live stock.
In addition to these major projects many small schemes have been developed by individual farmers, where it has been made possible to store run-off water which will be used to irrigate from five to twenty acres and in some instances up to eighty or one hundred acres on a farm. This is the best form of assistance, reestablishing and rehabilitating the farmer on his own land.
We have also in southwestern Saskatchewan the problem of sub-marginal lands. This was dealt with to some extent this afternoon by the hon. member for Wood Mountain, but I should like to say a few words concerning it. In the early years of this century during the rush for land in the great west, large areas of sub-marginal land were settled on. These lands to-day are not fit for growing cereals. The areas range in size from a few sections to blocks of thousands of acres. Owing to the type of soil and the lack of precipitation the people who settled on these lands have failed. Many of them failed even before the general drought that we are now experiencing.
The problem of what to do with this land confronts us. It has been decided to withdraw this land from cultivation and turn it into community pastures, assisting the settlers on these lands to reestablish themselves on better land as close to the pasture area as possible, where the development of a pasture will enable them to rehabilitate themselves. The development of community pastures in these areas will return the land to live stock production as a range area. This land is fenced and cross-fenced with suitable stock fences, the crossfences dividing the pasture into breeding reserves and main pastures. As these areas have for the most part been cultivated we find the land in various stages of grass; part of it has the natural prairie grass; the rest may be bare ground or drifting sand. It is therefore necessary to get the grass cover started as soon as possible. The pastures are operated under definite rules, particular attention being paid to prevent overgrazing. These grazing areas will be used for producing the best grades of beef cattle, using the best sires. By this method we hope to produce a uniform animal suitable for the eastern and overseas market. Sixteen of these pastures, varying in size from 6,000 to 25,000 acres, were completed in 1937.
This afternoon the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) outlined the policy of the agricultural improvement associations. I should like to say a few words concerning them as we have a number of these associations established in the constituency which I have the honour to represent, and they are accomplishing a great deal of good work. Their object is to encourage farmers in a community to cooperate in the solution of their own problems arising from drought and soil drifting, by the general adoption of such policies as strip farming, cover crops and cultural methods best suited to local conditions. These associations are supervised from the

Drought Area-Mr. Evans

experimental farm in the district. Free distribution of suitable drought resisting grass seed is made to members of the associations. In the past sweet clover, alfalfa, brome grass and crested wheat grass have been distributed to members. The seed so distributed is tp be used for seed production purposes, allowing each member to increase his own seed and also gain experience in producing seeded forage crops. Crested wheat grass has been most in demand through the drought areas, and has given promising results. Such organizations as these are necessary to assist the experimental farms in keeping contact with the farmers and to aid in the distribution of seed.
In conclusion I would say that we are advancing in the rehabilitation of the drought areas slowly but surely, keeping in view permanency in policy and getting full value for the money expended. We find that the development of the smaller irrigation projects is most satisfactory. I visited some of those projects that we heard about this afternoon down in Montana. I found that the project developed at Malta was a series of small irrigation projects taking the water out of one stream. I believe that the policy we are following in Saskatchewan in developing the small individual irrigation project is the thing which will reestablish and rehabilitate the drought area in that province.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
First I wish to place myself behind whatever sound means the government decides upon to rehabilitate the province of Saskatchewan. I have heard the cost mentioned here this afternoon, and while cost is always of importance, still I say whatever means the government decide are necessary to rehabilitate Saskatchewan should, irrespective of the cost, be supported unanimously by this country. The country cannot exist without Saskatchewan.
Now I am going to touch on another phase of this subject that has not been dealt with by any of the previous speakers. In a way I hesitate to do so, because, search as I might, on the one hand I have not found engineers to agree as to the real cause of the trouble, and on the other I have not found engineers to agree on the real source or origin of the moisture required for Saskatchewan. Some say one thing; some say another; but before entering upon that phase of what I have to say I should like to pass a word or two of comment on the remarks of one or two previous speakers. First, I refer to some remarks made by the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly). I thought he gave an exhaustive and clear explanation of what he

had in mind, and in the course of his remarks he asked a question in reference to something that had been said earlier by, I believe, the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch), in reference to the diversion of water from the North and South Saskatchewan rivers. At that time I believe I asked what was the cubic feet flow per second of water on either or both of these rivers, and the hon. member for Wood Mountain asked where the water was going to come from.
. That is a problem, Mr. Speaker. If the two Saskatchewan rivers are diverted, it will mean, of course, that the water from them will be lost as far as the rivers are concerned. The water might do splendid work in irrigation projects, but it would not return to the river. I thought it might be worth while just to say something about the flow per second of these two rivers. They vary very widely in their maximum and minimum. The mean average flow of the united Saskatchewan at The Pas, throughout the year 1934-35, October to September, was 22,700 cubic feet per second. The maximum flow was 55,700 cubic feet per second; but the minimum flow, with the water at its lowest point, was down to 3,960 cubic feet per second. The North Saskatchewan at Edmonton ranges from a maximum of 46,300 cubic feet per second to an average of 8,290 cubic feet per second and as low as 460 cubic feet per second as a minimum. So the question asked by the hon. member for Wood Mountain was a pertinent one, in my judgment, inasmuch as the diversions that were mentioned as being required for the irrigation of Saskatchewan were as follows:	The hon.
member for Acadia said that from the North Saskatchewan there should be a diversion of 6.800 cubic second feet; from the Clearwater river, 1,180 cubic feet per second; and from the Red Deer river, which I believe is a tributary of the South Saskatchewan, 2,275 cubic feet per second.
As I said a moment ago, the question asked by the hon. member for Wood Mountain was quite pertinent, for the total diversion flow that would be required, according to the bulletin entitled Reclamation Service, which was quoted by the hon. member for Acadia, would be over 10,000 cubic feet per second. So if there were a sustained diversion from the North and South Saskatchewan of anything like that number of cubic second feet, it would necessitate some measures to store up the water at the headwaters of those two rivers, as has been done in the state of Arizona irrigation projects. Large reservoirs would have to be built so that the flow could be maintained in all the seasons for which the water would be required.

Drought Area-Mr. MacNicol
Another hon. gentleman said something to the effect that it was not lack of moisture in Saskatchewan which was causing the trouble. If it is not a lack of moisture, then it must be a lack of rain. From time to time we have seen in the press the hopes of the people of Saskatchewan, and I might say of the whole world, for the prosperity of the world depends to a large extent upon the production of wheat. The Saskatchewan newspapers, during the wheat growing season, keep reporting, " If we only have rain, such and such will take place." I made a rather extended survey into what I would call the origin of the rainfall for Saskatchewan, but I have been unable to come to any definite conclusions as to the original source of the moisture which formed the clouds above that province. I remember reading the opinion of a former prominent official of this government, I believe in the meteorological service, a celebrated man and engineer. His impression, in which I found concurrence in Washington, was that the moisture which makes rainfall over Saskatchewan originates in the gulf of Mexico. Lately engineers have said that is not so. Others have said that the origin of that moisture is the Pacific ocean; that currents of air come over the Rocky mountains and meet other currents of air over Saskatchewan, and that thereby rain is formed. The engineer, to whom I referred a moment ago, held the opinion-which was shared by many others-that the warm currents of air coming from the gulf of Mexico up the Mississippi and Missouri valleys met colder currents of air over Saskatchewan, coming from the Arctic ocean and Hudson bay, and formed the rain which falls there. I have heard others say that the origin is Hudson bay.
The point I make, Mr. Speaker, is that apparently there is no definite engineering opinion as to the origin of the rainfall which Saskatchewan should and did have. For a long time I have been pursuing studies in connection with rainfall, precipitation and the water production of the St. Lawrence watershed. During the course of my investigations I have asked engineers if part of the rainfall that should and did fall in the province of Saskatchewan by any chance might originate in the great lakes watershed. There again I found there was no one who had a definite opinion. I venture an opinion-which may be entirely wrong, because every other man who has made a study of this seemingly has a different origin for the rainfall of Saskatchewan-that part of it might still be from the great lakes watershed just as well as from the gulf of Mexico, the Arctic ocean, Hudson
5X952-42J
bay or the Pacific ocean. It might be that all these might be sources of that rainfall. If the government wishes to make an investigation as to where the origin of moisture is for the supply of Saskatchewan, I assume it will have to send up some balloons capable of ascertaining the currents in the air in the upper stratosphere, and determine what can be done.
Whether or not the St. Lawrence watershed has supplied moisture to Saskatchewan is something which no one may tell. I know that on the earth's surface the current of air is eastward, but where is it when it is five thousand feet hivh in the air? No one can tell where the moisture originates; but if any part of it was from the watershed of the great lakes I am wondering whether the fact that over ten billion tons of water a year are taken out of the St. Lawrence watershed and poured into the Mississippi watershed could have anything whatever to do with the alteration in the amount of moisture, or could have any effect on the moisture which is said formerly to have come from the gulf of Mexico and part of which may have come from the watershed of the great lakes.
That suggestion may sound a little farfetched, and perhaps it is a long way from the subject of irrigation. However we do know that irrigation is one way of providing moisture, and that rainfall is the real and proper source of moisture. Apparently for a number of years past Saskatchewan has not had its proper share of rainfall, and I should think any body of engineers appointed by the government should endeavour to find out what has happened to the origin of the rainfall which formerly fell in Saskatchewan.
We know that in the St. Lawrence watershed there has been a gradual reduction in rainfall. Later on that fact may have a serious effect, so far as agriculture in Ontario and adjacent states is concerned. I find that at page 43 of John R. Freeman's book, which deals with the regulation of the great lakes, he states that the Canadian meteorological office has said that over a period of fifty years the reduction in rainfall in Ontario has been 2-3 inches, and that the equivalent weighted average reduction for the whole watershed is three inches. That is a colossal reduction. We know that to-day Saskatchewan is suffering from a lack of water, but it may be that in the course of time, unless some measures are taken to return the waters to their proper levels in their watersheds, the eastern provinces may be in a similar difficulty.
A committee sitting in Washington is now considering a measure to alter the judgment
Drought Area-Mr. MacNicol

of the United States Supreme Court handed down in 1930, in which the court directed that the diversion at Chicago should not exceed 1,500 second feet. The bill before the house asked that commencing in 1939 the provision for 1,500 second feet be changed to 5,000. In the proceedings before the committee one of the congressmen, Francis D. Culkin, quoted from a speech he made on January 18, 1934, in which he said:
It is no secret that most of this water has been used by Chicago in generating electricity for commercial purposes. God intended this water to flow east through the great lakes.
Its diversion was a larceny, pure and simple, and was destructive of every shore-front locality along the basin of the great lakes.
Worse than that, it has been one of the causes-there are several major causes-of the reduction equivalent to three inches in rainfall over the entire St. Lawrence watershed area. Whether or not that had any effect on the lack of rainfall in Saskatchewan, I cannot say.
Certainly it is true that water finds its own level, and I suppose clouds, in their flight through the air, are partly affected by the water on the surface. I would say that this whole interference with nature which has been going on for so many years has had a much greater effect throughout Canada and the United States with respect to the amount of rainfall and drought than any person knows. The time has come to make a serious investigation.
Whatever investigation the government may determine to make-and I believe it should make one, in addition to what it is now doing- it should deal with the problem of diversion from the great lakes. I believe the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) and the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) reported that the work which has been done in the west has been beneficial. If the storage of water is beneficial in the west, it would be equally beneficial to make an endeavour to return the great lakes of the east to their former natural water levels.
In Washington a few days ago, in connection with this very matter, namely the gradual lowering of the water level of the great lakes, there was a suggestion to build control works across the Niagara river, in order to raise the level of lake Erie, and control works at the outlet of lake Huron, on the St. Clair river, in order to raise the water levels of lakes Huron and Michigan, which are really one lake. This latter is a lake area of 45.000 square miles which is to-day three feet plus, lower than the average level of those
[Mr MacNicol.]
lakes for the forty year period between 1860 and 1900. That is a very serious loss of water to the central portion of this continent.
By such works it is possible that the water levels could be returned to their former point, but it would take a long time to do this. If it were returned, evaporation would be greater and, if evaporation on the great lakes has anything whatever to do with rainfall beyond the great lakes watershed, or if it has anything to do with the rainfall east or west of that watershed, no doubt the increased level would be beneficial to the areas adjacent thereto.
May I point out that in this part of the country we are threatened with further diversions of water from northern Ontario, a matter which may or may not affect the rainfall. I take the same stand as that taken by the congressman a few days ago, when he quoted his own speech of 1934, in which he said that God intended the water to flow in one direction. In my judgment man has not any business to divert a large volume of water from one watershed to another.
In the west the diversion of the waters of the two Saskatchewan rivers would not be a diversion from one watershed to another. If there is any possible way of diverting the water of either the North Saskatchewan or the South Saskatchewan rivers for irrigation to benefit the people of Saskatchewan, I for one would support it. However, in view of what I have heard to the effect that the water level is away below the ground level, it would appear that dams, windmills or something of the kind would be necessary to elevate the water. That is not the old system of irrigation which has been handed down from the earliest days.
Egypt diverts water from the Nile north of the first cataract Between that point and the sea is a distance of some five to six hundred miles, and for all that distance the adjacent land is almost level. The river flows quite gently and all they have to do is to tap the water and let it run all over the land. It would be quite a task to pump water up as high as has been suggested by the hon. member for Wood Mountain. It would be much easier if the water could be allowed just to run down hill.
Some hon. member mentioned Holland. I investigated the irrigation projects in that country this summer.

Drought Area-Mr. Rowe (Athabaska)
I investigated 200 square miles of that country. The rivers running from southeast to Rotterdam flow above the land level, but they explained to me that where the subsidiary canals run alongside the main canals they have pumping outfits. Sometimes the water is pumped from the land and on other days it may be pumped back, depending upon the amount of evaporation. Whether or not this actually happens, I cannot say, but that is how it was explained to me. I can see that where you are able to have the water run down hill, your irrigation problems would be much easier to solve than if you have to pump it up.
I rose merely to say that is a too tremendous problem for Saskatchewan to tackle alone. That province has suffered tremendously during the last few years, far beyond wwhat any province should be called upon to suffer. I know in the judgment of the government, this is a national problem. The services of the best engineers, both in and out of Canada, should be obtained and then parliament should consider what is necessary in order that a sincere effort may be made to rehabilitate that great province. When I was home on Saturday I attended a meeting, the report of which will come out later. I shall not say just what meeting it was, but mention was made of the large number of people returning from Saskatchewan to Ontario. I know that some relations of mine who have been farming in Saskatchewan for twenty-five years and have helped to build up that country have had to return to Ontario after losing all they had. While it is no disgrace for anyone to lose all he has after going through six or seven years of depression, the fact is that these people are back here and will have to be taken care of. In that way this matter becomes an Ontario problem. I shall close with the suggestion that the government obtain the best advice possible, which I believe it will do, and then set out to do all that can be done to rehabilitate Saskatchewan. In that I am sure they will have the support of all parties in the house.

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution now under discussion reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should place before parliament at an early date plans, or proposals, for a comprehensive and authoritative survey of water conservation, irrigation possibilities, and other feasible projects for the permanent rehabilitation of the drought stricken area of western Canada and its people.
First, I wish to congratulate the mover of the resolution upon having brought this matter
before parliament. I think the remarks made to-day and the diversified opinions expressed only tend to emphasize the necessity for a survey of this problem being made by technically competent experts so that the people of Canada will know once and for all the attainable possibilities of irrigation in western Canada. Western Canada is one of the world's greatest grain growing areas, but recurring drought periods have brought ruin to a multitude of farmers and those dependent upon them. If it is possible to restore this world's granary to its former potential productivity, and it is within the power of parliament to bring about this result, it automatically becomes the unescapable legal and moral duty of parliament to bring about that result.
To a layman-and I am speaking as such- all the factors favourable to the accomplishment of such a purpose appear to be present. There can be no doubt as to the fertility and crop producing qualities of the soil of western Canada. During the recent drought years I had occasion to revisit sections of the prairie country which had been known to me personally in the early days to be capable of producing large crops. I had seen heavy yields in the plain country around Regina and I was shocked when I went there a few years later to discover that those areas had reverted to veritable deserts.
To a layman it appears that nowhere on this planet has nature been so lavish in the provision of abundant water supplies as on the eastern slopes of the Rocky mountains. Springing from great glaciers and melting snows high up among the peaks and valleys of the Rockies there are innumerable streams and great rivers like the Oldman, the Bow, the Red Deer, the North Saskatchewan and the Athabaska. It so happens that rising temperatures and the early summer melting of mountain snows bring down to the plains vast volumes of water just when the growing crops are most in need of moisture. Writing in the Regina Daily Star of January 22, 1938, Mr. H. H. Cleugh, a gentleman who has made a study of this question, suggests that these rivers should be dammed at a sufficient level above the plains to permit of gravity flow. This is a phase of the matter which has not been touched upon extensively during this debate. In view of the fact that Mr. Cleugh appears to have made a study of this matter, I think it is advisable to place upon Hansard one or two of the statements he has made in the Regina Daily Star.
He states that this water could be carried by gravity to the plains surrounding Regina.
662	COMMONS
Drought Area-Mr. Rowe (Athabaska)
Then he suggests tapping the Bow river at Glenbow, which is 1,500 feet above the city of Regina. As that point is 500 miles away, this would mean a fall of three feet to the mile. He stated also that the Saskatchewan people lost over $120,000,000 in 1937 through seed and labour thrown away on crops which failed because of the drought. Mr. Cleugh believes that for less than that amount pipe lines could have been built and sufficient water brought down to turn southern Saskatchewan into a swamp in two years. I am going to quote from his article as he includes in it some of the figures referred to a moment ago by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol).
I have looked into this very carefully and find in June the amount passing Medicine Hat is
26.000	cubic second feet. Now here is power and also a lot of water for irrigation if a suitable dam site can be found and a pumping station established but I have little hope of pumps.
But that is not all and pumping is not in it compared to the natural law of gravity. The Bow river can be harnessed at Glenbow above Calgary and have 1,500 feet fall to Regina and
10.000	cubic second feet of water can be harnessed in a pipe line with an average fall of three feet to a mile, through the 500 miles of distance; 500 to 600 cubic second feet can be delivered through one pipe line and there is enough water to fill 20 pipes of a 12-foot diameter intake; enough water can be had to make Saskatchewan a swamp in two years if the water is held there.
A 12-foot intake with a fall like that would irrigate one inch deep over 60,000 acres a week and there is enough water running to waste at that point to irrigate about three acres one inch deep every second. Then there are the Maeleod, the north Saskatchewan and Red Deer rivers high enough above Saskatoon, Regina and Broadview to deliver another 12,000 cubic second feet by gravity alone at a terrific speed. In other words in four rivers you have enough water to irrigate one inch deep, six acres every second, or 21 million acres one inch deep in 40 days and in the Bow river alone enough water to irrigate 21 million acres in 90 days, and all that volume will run down without pumping to where it is needed.
Saskatchewan undoubtedly has the water necessary for irrigation and lots of it, but let us suppose for a few moments we irrigated not 21 million acres but 10 million acres every 15 days and instead of 10 bushels to the acre we got 40 bushels, would we not save time, labour and machinery?
Instead of growing wheat only we could grow corn, sorghum, millet, sugar beets, winter rye, sunflowers and alfalfa for siloes, turning out hogs instead of just wheat. Let us farm and no longer be a band of destructive pirates. Make burning straw piles a crime, and burning over prairie or stubble field, bluff and slough, a penalty of not less than five years of hard labour or a $5,000 fine. Burning the prairie especially in the fall has burned the humus which acted the same as a sponge in holding the precipitation. Not only that but the grass roots in the humus covered the ground from
fMr. P. J. Rowe.]
wind, and there were no dust storms until the land became pulverized and the straw and stubble burned and no humus left and no fibre to break the wind or hold the soil together.
All of that sounds to a mere layman very alluring indeed. I do not know whether it is correct or not; but I suggest there is a way to find out, without costing the government very much, and that is to have an authoritative survey made so that all these differences of opinion and arguments pro and con which we have been hearing can be finally cleared up. If Mr. Cleugh is right and we can irrigate southern Saskatchewan and southern Alberta from the South Saskatchewan and Bow rivers, immediately we think of possibilities in central and northern Alberta and Saskatchewan by using the waters of the Red Deer river and the North Saskatchewan river.
There are also the possibilities of generating electric power. That is one point which has not been touched upon. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) in the terms of his resolution suggests " other feasible projects," and I submit the prospect of generating electric power might well be investigated very carefully. In that connection, Mr. Speaker, there is the suggestion that auxiliary power could be generated by steam. We have unlimited quantities of coal in Alberta, over eighty-seven per cent of the coal in Canada, and if the minimum flow of these rivers in the winter time was such that there was not sufficient water power to generate the electricity required, we could switch to steam. I am referring to the possibilities of generating electricity because, after all, if it is possible to bring electric power and electric appliances into domestic use on the prairies, the farmers of western Canada have a right to have them.
How is such a project to be paid for? I am quite aware that we cannot introduce in the house resolutions which involve the expenditure of money, and I want to make it quite clear that I am only trying to suggest something constructive in the event of a survey being made. We have to envisage or forecast the possible means of paying for such a project if the government decides to undertake it.
The other day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning) laid on the table the latest returns of the Canadian chartered banks. The total savings reported were 81,580,000,000, held by 4,084,752 people; but, notice, 3,770,000 of these people have an average of only $120 in their savings accounts, while the other 314,740 have 81,127,500,000 in their savings accounts. I notice further that 536 persons have in their savings accounts an average of $287,500 each. It is safe to say that there

Drought Area-Mr. Rowe (Athabaska)
are not many western farmers, or fishermen, or workers in the last class. If we recall the many references which have been made to the brief submitted by the present Minister of Labour (Mr. Rogers) to the royal commission that sat in the maritime provinces, the three prairie provinces in 1931 were forced to pay in increased living costs because of the tariff something like $56,000,000. That was due to the tariff protection enjoyed by eastern manufacturers. It would be interesting to discover if there is any connection between that $56,000,000 of increased living costs and the average of $287,500 held by 536 people in eastern savings accounts, and to ascertain where they got that money. I suppose if their wages were equal to the wages of farmers and office boys, $350 a year as suggested by the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Deachman) it would take them about eight hundred years to earn that amount, and about eight thousand years to save it, because you cannot lay by very much in the way of savings out of $350 a year.
I have this suggestion to make. While the Minister of Labour does not, I think, agree with the tariff protection idea, he said that if we abolished the tariff, confederation would be endangered. The inference I drew from that was that the western producers are expected to submit to a levy of $56,000,000 every year in order that confederation may live. That is quite a sacrifice to ask them to make. I suggest that no institution, confederation or anything else, can exist very long on a shaky foundation of that kind, and that the greatest danger to confederation to-day is just these very injustices that one group in this country imposes upon another.
One way to correct that, I think, would be this: I am assuming that such an irrigation and electrification scheme would cost $400,000,000. Suppose the dominion government were to offer a bond issue of $400,000,000 at two per cent payable serially in ten years; the annual amount required to retire the principal would be $40,000,000 and the annual interest would be $8,000,000. This $48,000,000 would still be $8,000,000 short of the annual tribute exacted by eastern protected manufacturers against the three prairie provinces. How would it be, to compensate the west in part for the wrongs they have suffered, if the entire amount of such bond issue were recovered through an excess profits tax? I believe that nothing less than a tangible act of this kind, with a complete rearrangement for the future, can heal the wounds which have already been inflicted, and strengthen again ties which at this moment are perilously near the breaking point.
I have no doubt that such a loan would be quickly taken up, as it would earn more than the one and a half per cent which the banks now pay to these people, and with the Dominion of Canada behind it the security would be unquestioned. I need hardly add that I am making this suggestion merely as an interim measure, because I am confident that in ten years from now the interest system will have been discovered to be one of the principal stumbling blocks in the path of social progress, and will either have been replaced by a more scientific and equitable one, or be just about ready for the scrap heap, and this, too, without placing in jeopardy the security of any person.
It occurs to me that there are eight points which might be gained by this proposal. May I outline them:
(1)	It would make available an abundant and never-failing water supply to the farmers of the prairie plains, thereby bringing to them permanent security.
(2)	It would make possible diversified farming, where, in addition to wheat, sorghum, millet, sugar beets, winter rye, sunflowers, and corn could be grown, and this would make possible hog and chicken raising as well as a vastly greater volume of dairy products, rendering the prairies self-sustaining in all these commodities, with a large export surplus.
(3)	A public work of this magnitude would provide for the unemployed in western Canada.
(4)	It would make available electric light and power for industrial and domestic appliances, adding greatly to the comfort and convenience of the homes of Canadian western farmers, workers and fishermen.
(5)	It would not add to the cost of living of the workers, farmers or fishermen in either eastern or western Canada.
(6)	It would effectively level out and check the effect of falling prices in the approaching depression, by increasing work, permanent assets and purchasing power.
(7)	It would strengthen confederation and alleviate one of the principal causes of strained relationships between the east and the west at the present time.
(8)	It would focus the attention of the Canadian people on a project into which we could direct our energies, now being wasted in the perpetuation of a stupid, archaic competitive system which, unless we check its mad, chaotic course, will soon lead the world into war. And another world war would mean the suicide of civilization.
May I for a moment examine the economic consequences of an irrigation and electrification plan such as I have proposed. One of the
664	COMMONS
Drought Area-Mr. Rowe (Athabaska)
anomalies of our present system is that a universally good crop is a calamity, and when the children in our great cities cry for bread we say, "No, you can't have any, because we've got too much." In the United States to-day, after years of earnest but futile endeavour, they have reached the tragic stage where there are more than 12,000,000 unemployed, and the proposed crop restriction and curtailment plans of the government will inevitably aggravate the heart-breaking and impossible prices of food and clothing, prices under which an ill-clad, under-paid and undernourished working class must falter and fall.
The world wheat conference which met in London last month warned the wheat growers of the world that there was imminent danger of an over-supply of wheat, and that this would mean a disastrous fall in price. I have no doubt that some of my hon. friends who pride themselves on being practical and realistic will oppose this plan on the ground that we must keep things scarce in order to keep up the price. Well, ,if that is being realistic I must define a realist as one who insists upon repeating the errors of his ancestors. Then it may be opportune to ask, Who really is the farmers' friend? The government or the sawfly? The government spends a great deal of money in laboratory research trying to find ways of combating the rust, the boll-weevil, the corn-borer and the saw-fly; but, after all, are these humble parasites not really carrying out the policy of the government by restricting production?
I am ready to agree that the establishment of an adequate irrigation system in the prairie provinces would increase the volume of wheat, coarse grains, live stock and dairy products for sale on world markets, but it would at the same time guarantee an unfailing food supply for the hundreds of millions of people in India and China who are constantly on the edge of starvation and never know what it means to eat more than once each day. This, of course, means that we must change our system from one of production for profit to one of production for use.
The present competitive system, in its efforts to keep things scarce in order to keep up the price, results in the astonishing spectacle of individuals, groups and nations actually competing with one another, for things which may be had in abundance without competition. This false scarcity philosophy results in striving, hate, tariffs to keep things scarce, jealousy, envy and murder, finally culminating in mankind's worst collective social crime, war, where the internationally

recognized vice of private murder, if multiplied sufficiently until it becomes mass murder and mutual extermination, is elevated to the honour and glory of a virtue.
May I say in closing, Mr. Speaker, that all those things which exalt and embellish our civilized life-art, science, philosophy and religion-had their roots in those ancient civilizations and empires which were cradled in the valleys of the Nile, the Euphrates, the Indus and the Hwang-ho, whose life-giving streams have flowed eternally down from the snow-covered ranges of Africa and Asia. They built their pyramids, conduits, palaces and temples with human hands, unassisted by nature. All too often their sumptuous palaces were built by slaves to gratify the vanity and ambition of thieves and robbers, otherwise known as kings and emperors, and the backs that bore the burdens also bore the marks of the slave-drivers lash. We, in this enlightened age, also have slaves at our command, but not the degredation and humiliation of human slavery. We have countless thousands of wild horses, rushing down the gorges of our mighty mountain rivers, ready to be tamed and harnessed in the service of humanity. Shall we use them? These ancient peoples sometimes spent years or generations in building their public works, but they had more intelligence than we moderns because they did not shackle succeeding generations with debt and interest. When these public works were created they were paid for.
It should be clear by every process of logic and by the proof of historic fact that the wealth of a nation, the character of its people, the quality and permanence of its institutions are all dependent upon a sound and sufficient agricultural foundation. Not armies or navies, or commerce, or diversity of manufacture, or anything other than the farm is the anchor which hold through the storms of time that sweep all else away.
