speechtext:
I had not intended to make any remarks in reference to the resolution before the house had it not been for the speech of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Massey). He carried us back to the days of confederation, 1867, and he divided Canada into east and west with the dividing line at the western end of the great province of Ontario. While sitting here I thought of the words, "Lest we forget." I do not know of any occasion on which they are more apt or should be recalled with more seriousness or deeper human sympathy than

Drought Area-Mr. Finn
on this very day, because conditions in the world art such that we need to stop and think, "Lest we forget."
Just thirty-eight years ago to-day I sailed from Halifax on the steamship Milwaukee for South Africa and the Boer war. Arriving at Table bay twenty-eight days out from Halifax we went on board the tender to go ashore, along with Colonel Evans, Major Williams, Lieutenant Van Straubenze, who was a soldier and a man and who was killed in the great war, 1914-1918, and a clergyman from Lunenburg who was chaplain to the First and Second Canadian Mounted Rifles, a minister of the Methodist church who did very much for the boys on board that ship from the day she left the port of Halifax until we were at Ellfontein, sixteen miles northwest of Pretoria. As I was standing on the deck of the tender going ashore a gentleman who held the rank of colonel came up to me. He saw "Canada" on my shoulder and said, "I see you are from Canada." I said, "Yes, sir, I am." He said, "I am Colonel Doctor Conan Doyle." I said, "I have read some of your books." He said, "I am here with the Doctor Langham hospital corps, trying to look after the convalescents who come down from the front."
We went through that great country of Cape Colony up to the Orange river where the bridge had been blown up; that great iron structure looked like a lot of snakes. It was a Canadian who built across that river a transportation bridge over which men and ammunition might be taken into the Orange Free State. That engineer was Colonel Girouard, son of Hon. Mr. Justice Girouard of the Supreme Court of Canada. When the mules were passing over, kicking up like the very old Harry, at least I felt happy to know that the way was made safe, not for democracy, but for us to cross without falling into the water. After crossing the river where President Steyn was fighting up to his middle in the water, we went on to Bloemfontein, and just outside Bloemfontein I met a fellow Haligonian, Captain Harry Stair, who came up and spoke to me. The chaplain of whom I spoke was the Reverend Mr. Lane from Lunenburg. I pay him this tribute, because he was as broad as the sky above us on a clear night, and the work he did had an uplifting and inspiring influence on every man aboard that ship from Captain Webster down to the humblest sailor and the humblest individual going to the war, which was myself.
From there we went into the Transvaal, among the mighty mountains where we did
not know at what moment we were going to receive that reward which comes to a soldier or a war correspondent. We arrived at Johannesburg, where doors were barred and windows shuttered; from there we went on to Pretoria, and met Lord Roberts and Lord Kitchener, both now deceased, and saw the home of Oom Paul Kruger, a sentry with fixed bayonets outside, and Mrs. Kruger and some Boers sitting on the verandah. Oom Paul had gone by fast train, blowing the bridges behind him, to Delagoa bay, where he took a ship for Holland, where my good friend (Mr. MacNieol) was last summer, where he found that there were waters flowing and something else that flowed, I am not sure what they call it but I think it is Holland gin.
But, Mr. Speaker, to be serious, I speak of February 21, 1900, because at that time England and the empire were fighting the Boers. To-day some say, "Well, has not England been an aggressor?" I say in that respect, "No." Why? Because on the subjugation of that country it was handed back to them. To-day it is one mighty confederation, and the very men, General Hertzog, Smuts and other generals, who would have shot Queen Victoria on sight, have become the leaders of that confederation and sit in the councils of the empire in London at the imperial conferences of this commonwealth of nations. These changes, Mr. Speaker, are of a kind that make one wonder why conditions are as they are to-day in reference to matters of national and international concern, with which I do not propose to deal for one moment. But I say, "Lest we forget."
Let me say that I am in hearty accord with the aspirations of hon. gentlemen in this house who come from the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. They have had their drought seasons; influences have been brought to bear that have made their country not so happy to live in as the older provinces which entered into confederation in 1867. I am not an engineer; therefore I am not in a position to deal with the question of irrigation or its cost or the portions of the country where it is necessary. But I do say this, that I believe this government is sympathetic to the interests of those provinces which were carved out by the late great leader of the Liberal party, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and it will see to it that as far as it can and as far as the treasury will provide, those conditions will be ameliorated, so that the present hardships may be forgotten and happiness may reign again among our people in the west.
That brings me, sir, to the little province of Nova Scotia, that rock-ribbed province
Drought Area-Mr. Finn

which gave to Canada that magnificent maritime frontage on the east without which Canada could not have been a nation. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, and hon. gentlemen who sit in the house for the first time, that we were taken into confederation-I was not born then-against our will. To-day we are satisfied to be a part of this great Canada of ours, extending from Halifax to Vancouver; but we are most desirous, yea, insistent, that the promises and pledges which were given to us, not by word of mouth but by statute shall be carried out, perhaps not to the letter, because we are not after our pound of flesh, but we are after that which will bring the prosperity that should be ours as the eastern gateway of this young country.
The British North America Act of 1867 provided in section 145 for the construction of the Intercolonial railway from the city of Halifax to a point on the St. Lawrence river. That railway was built at a cost of millions of dollars, which was contributed by England. That railway was constructed to our disadvantage. Why? Because the British government insisted that it be built so far away from the American border so that if there was another war between England and the United States our line of communication could not be cut. So the road was built down around the bay of Chaleur, and on to Moncton and through to Halifax, making the line about two hundred miles longer than it should have been if it had been built as the Canadian Pacific railway was, though not through the state of Maine, as is the Canadian Pacific, from Megantic and then on through the province of New Brunswick to Saint John. We were sufferers because of that, and the disadvantages were such and the rail haul was so great that the opportunity was given the Canadian Pacific to construct a shorter line. As Sir Charles Tupper said, he bought a summer place at St. Andrews, New Brunswick, because he could come down from Montreal to St. Andrews in twelve hours, whereas it would take him about sixty hours to get there by road, because the Intercolonial railway was not completed to the city of Halifax. Those were the conditions, and it took many years to have the government realize that those conditions could no longer continue; that we should carry Canadian goods over Canadian railways and out through Canadian ports, on both the Atlantic and the Pacific.
Then in 1903 there was placed upon the statute books of Canada the Transcontinental Railway Act which assured to the people of Canada, east, west and in the centre, a line of railway coming through from Vancouver to Edmundston and from Edmundston down

to Moncton as a common centre for Halifax and Saint John, reducing our mileage by about 150 miles. Under that contract, sir, it was provided that the Grand Trunk should operate that line of railway; that they should build piers; that they should build or charter ships and that they should carry every bit of freight, unless specifically routed otherwise, through Canadian ports.

speechtext:
The discussion this afternoon and evening has been both interesting and instructive, and as seconder of the motion I should like to spend only a few moments in dealing with some of the objections that have been raised by some of those who have spoken to this motion. I think those objections may be classified, roughly, under two headings: First, the objection of those who point out that there is now being carried on under the prairie farm rehabilitation administration all the work necessary and, second, the objection of those who feel that irrigation and water conservation are not feasible.
I want to deal with those two objections, and first with reference to the matter of the prairie farm rehabilitation administration. The hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) -and I need not repeat what he said-outlined ten objectives of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I draw the attention of the house to the fact that those ten objectives have to do with such things as substations for experimental farms, farm improvement associations, reclamation stations and soil survey, all of which are for the purpose of gathering data and securing information.
The prairie farm rehabilitation administration has done excellent work in mapping out the general course that a program of rehabilitation ought to take, but it has not had sufficient funds at any time to put on, on a large scale, the program necessary to meet the problem of drought in the prairie provinces. In the discussion which took place last year on the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, along with other members from the west I commended what had been done under that administration. But I submit that the figures given this afternoon by the hon. member for Swift Current show that the prairie farm rehabilitation administration is, more or less, dealing in a "penny ante" way with the question of drought. The figures in connection with dug-outs would seem to indicate this contention. There have been 11,000 applications, 5,500 of which have been approved and only 4,300 completed. The hon. member for Swift Current said-and I take this to be pretty well the general attitude of the government-"It is better to get people to assist themselves than to have large scale expenditures by the government." I took his words down, but he may correct me if in any way I have misquoted him. I believe that would seem to describe the prairie farm rehabilitation program. It is an attitude whereby the people are asked to assist themselves to meet a problem of drought. I would point out, however, that when you
ask the people in a drought area to assist themselves you are asking them to try to lift themselves by tugging at their own shoelaces. You ask a man to put in a dugout or a dam for eight cents a cubic yard when, as the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) pointed out, it takes at least twelve cents, if not more. It means that he must have horses -and a lot of farmers have no horses. It means extra feed for those horses, because they have to work. If they use farm machinery it means fuel consumption. The same is true of planting grass seed. The fact that the farmers have not horses or feed for horses, and that they have not fuel for their tractors makes it impossible to carry out many of the excellent schemes suggested in the rehabilitation program.
The prairie farm rehabilitation administration has done excellent work. It has surveyed the field, and as a result of its work I think we shall not make mistakes which would have been made, had they not done the preparatory work. But I feel that -the resolution calls for a thorough investigation of the feasibility of water conservation, irrigation and other means of combating drought, and that those matters ought to be considered thoroughly by a competent body.
I come now to the second objection, namely that such a scheme is not feasible. I am not a civil engineer, nor was any hon. member who spoke this afternoon. The hon. member for Swift Current said it had been authoritatively stated that irrigation in Saskatchewan was not feasible. For proof, he quoted Mr. John Val-lance the head of the prairie farm rehabilitation administration, and the liaison officer Hon. George Spence, but may I point out that neither of these gentlemen is a civil engineer.
I suppose it would be possible for hon. members on both sides of the house to quote engineers, both pro and con, and still not get anywhere. The motion does suggest, however, that we as laymen shall neither sneer at the projects nor become eulogistic about them, but that we should endeavour to secure the best possible professional advice as to the feasibility of water conservation on the prairies.
With that in mind I should like to deal with my impression of the feasibility of these projects. I am thinking now of what is being carried on just across the international boundary between the United States and the Canadian drought area. In the last two years I have made it my business to make frequent trips into the area south of the border. I have gone into North Dakota, South Dakota and Montana, and have studied what the
668	COMMONS
Drought Area-Mr. Douglas (Weybum)
Americans are doing under their rehabilitation plan. I am cognizant of the fact that they are spending sums of money out of all proportion to the sums we are in a position to spend. Their population is much more dense, and the government has been willing to put large sums of money at the disposal of their engineers. But when one talks about the feasibility of what is being done there one can only speak of what he has seen of what is actually being done. Sometimes I have spent a week at a time with some of their engineers, visiting their different projects, receiving explanations of what they are doing and going into the homes of their people. The engineers explain that they are working on two principles, the first of which is that the drought is a recurring problem. They say that there have been droughts in the past, and that it is reasonable to expect that there will be droughts in the future. They say, further, that now during a period of drought, is the time when it is easiest to persuade governments and people concerned to look into the question of recurring drought.
To that end they are now setting up the necessary means whereby, when the moisture does return, they will be able to conserve it against the needs of future drought periods which they know are bound to come. The second principle on which they are working is one which was not mentioned this afternoon, namely, that the problem cannot be attacked on one front. It must be attacked on a number of fronts. They say quite frankly that there are large areas where irrigation is not feasible. There are some areas in which one procedure will solve the problem, and there are others where that same procedure is not a solution.
With that in mind I wish to outline the three main lines of approach which they have used. The first has to do with water conservation itself. In that connection they have spent money in putting in dams to hold bodies of water in rivers and creeks, and to prevent run-offs. By this means they have succeeded in having creeks backed up into gullies and sloughs, and have succeeded in holding bodies of water in the little hills of northern Montana and in supplying water-holes for the stock. A number of large dams have been built. Some of the engineers state frankly that if they were doing this work over again they would not build some of the very large dams on which huge sums of money have been spent. For instance, they say Fort Peck dam, which is a flood control project rather than an irrigation dam, has cost well over $100,000,000. They state they

would have been further ahead if they had built a number of smaller dams. More would have been accomplished with a smaller expenditure of money. But they are learning from the mistakes they have made.
The result is that they are conserving bodies of water. For instance, the engineers estimate that the Fort Peck dam will create a lake with a shore line of 1,600 miles and a body of water which will have an effect on climatic conditions. It will be possible for ranchers to water their stock. It will cause creeks to back up and fill the gullies. They have also gone in for small, individual dams, of which large numbers have been built. This has not been done on the basis of trying "to assist the farmer to assist himself." They have put out gangs of men on a daily wage basis. A gang would be moved on to a farm to build a dam and then move on to another farm, to build another. They have done the same thing in connection with building dugouts. They use drag-line dredges. I saw many cases where they had moved on to a farm and put in a dug-out in a day and a half. Then another gang would come along and plant trees around it, and then move on to the next farm. In the minds of many people water conservation means irrigation and irrigation only. In my opinion, the problem of water conservation is, if anything, more important than the question of irrigation.
The second method they have used is to irrigate. Wherever feasible they have irrigated the land. The hon. member for Maple Creek (Mr. Evans) and others have mentioned the project around Malta, Montana. I went around the Malta country with Superintendent Lantz and saw where they had taken land that was considered hopeless, paid the farmer $3 an acre for it and then proceeded to irrigate it. Under their housing scheme model homes were built with running water and electric lights. The land was cut up into small farms of from sixty to 120 acres and rented out on a thirty to forty years amortization basis.
Of course the best proof of any pudding is in the eating. I went to the home of a man by the name of Karl Blount, just outside Malta. He had been two years on a sixty-five acre farm and he showed me his books. His sugar beet crop alone had netted him $3,000 that year. His wheat had averaged over forty bushels to the acre. He had corn seven feet high and he thought it would run about sixty bushels to the acre. He had taken off several crops of alfalfa and had more feed than he could use. He claimed he had made more money in both the years he had been on that small farm than he had made

Drought Area-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
in any year he had been, on his old farm consisting of one section of land. Of course this is not feasible everywhere, but they are doing it wherever possible.
In other places they have combined dry farming and irrigated farming. They have irrigated a strip of land which has been broken up into plots of up to twenty acres, each with a new house. The farmer grows his feed for his stock and his garden stuff for his family on this irrigated plot, and .then back from the irrigated strip he has his huge dry area where he puts in his wheat crop. If his wheat crop should prove a failure he has a guarantee of his garden stuff and feed for his stock. They are trying to meet the problem in the different localities in different ways, depending upon the topography of the country and the economic conditions under which the people live.
I think when we pooh-pooh the idea of irrigation, we perhaps do so too quickly. A famous engineer went through western Canada last year and his reports of conditions were published in the press. One of his statements was that an irrigation project at Riverhurst, Saskatchewan, bringing water down from Moose Jaw to the Weyburn and Souris river would irrigate 7,000,000 acres of the drought lands of southern Saskatchewan at a cost of between 820,000,000 and 825,000,000. I am not in a position to say that that is a correct estimate as I am not a civil engineer like the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling) and one or two others.

speechtext:
The Bow river project to irrigate Alberta and Saskatchewan. I do not intend to go into that, but that was the one.
The third method used in the United States rehabilitation plan was that used in the areas where water conservation and irrigation were not so feasible, and where supplies of water were not available. In those areas they went
in for an extensive program of soil drifting prevention. Some hon. members have referred already to the manner in which they tackled this problem by planting crested wheat grass, brome grass and in some cases, soya beans, and also by strip farming. Of course this meant the expenditure of money. I went into one farm just a few miles out of the town of Plentywood, Montana. The soil on this farm had been reduced almost to black sand. The government inspector approved the farmer putting it into crested wheat grass. He put in 300 acres of this, for which the government paid him $7 an acre or a total of $2,100. This meant two things for that man. He was able to finance his operations this year without going on relief and, second, he was rehabilitating his farm.
All though the drought area the United States government has been paying farmers $3 an acre to put in summer fallow in fifteen rod strips. This makes it possible for a farmer to buy feed and carry out some of the suggestions we are always making in circulars, but which we never tell the farmer how to implement.
Before I sit down I should like to say that if such a program of water conservation, of irrigation and of soil erosion prevention could be undertaken, especially during these periods of drought, it would have a twofold beneficial effect. First of all, it would put us in a position to meet the next drought more intelligently and more successfully than we have met the present one. I cannot understand the attitude of some hon. members who keep pooh-poohing the whole idea of trying to deal with this problem from the scientific angle. If the medical men of this country were to inform us that we were to be subjected to the ravages of a certain disease at regular periods, we would organize all the resources of medical science to meet that condition. But when we know perfectly well that periods of drought will come which will upset our economy and cause our people to suffer privation and hardship, we simply sit back and say, "Well some day it will rain." But some day it will stop raining again and unless we are prepared to use the intelligence that we have to meet such a contingency we shall go through these years of suffering again and our children shall go through them after us.
The second beneficial effect would be that money would be spent on wages rather than on relief. The farmers and the unemployed in the small towns and villages could be paid wages. Both in and out of the house we hear mention made of the racketeering that goes on in relief. We hear of the fellow who has
670	COMMONS
Drought Area-Mr. Douglas (Weyburn)
a little tea dollar radio to which he dares to listen. There may be some racketeering, but I believe it is quite small. In my opinion the great mass of Canadian people who are compelled to take government assistance would far rather work for anything they get. I believe we could give them work by setting them to the task of building these dams and dugouts.
Late one night I was going to New Glasgow, Montana, with a number of friends in my car. Not being sure of the road, we stopped to inquire of a farmer just how we could get to New Glasgow. After directing us, he found out that we came from Canada and we stopped to chat. We asked him if he had any crop and he told us he had none at all. We then asked him how he lived, and he told us he had these sheep. One of the gentlemen with me said, "You cannot live on the products of a few sheep." He replied, "Oh, I work on the government WPA." We then asked how much it netted him. "Well," he said, "it varies. We get ten days a month, and some months I get more. My cheque last month was $98.80." The gentleman with me asked, "Is that charged up against your property?" He looked as though we had come from another sphere. "No," he said, "that is wages; I work for it."
There are thousands upon thousands of farmers in the drought area to-day who would like to say, "It is wages; I work for it." And such could be done, Mr. Speaker. We talk to-day about spending money for many other purposes which in my opinion would not give us as great a return in terms of human happiness and future prosperity as spending our money to conserve water against future periods of drought.

speakeroldname: Hon. T. A. CRERAR (Minister of Mines and Resources):
subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the discussion this afternoon and evening on this interesting subject has covered a very wide range. It has gone all the way from the Orange Free State to the great American desert, and from the head waters of the Athabaska to the watershed of the St. Lawrence river. That, I suppose, may be taken as an evidence of the importance of the subject and of the general interest it arouses.
If this problem could be solved by theoretical discussions, then I think the speaker who preceded me (Mr. Douglas) could make a useful contribution to its solution. But, Mr. Speaker, it is a practical problem, a very practical problem, and it must be so regarded.
The mover of the resolution (Mr. Cold-well) states in its terms that there should be "a comprehensive and authoritative survey of water conservation, irrigation possibilities,
[Mr. Douglas.)
and other feasible projects" looking to a permanent rehabilitation of the drought-stricken area. In that respect it is interesting to review what has been done in the way of meeting the proposals contained in the resolution. My hon. friend in his opening remarks quoted from Palliser's report and from the reports of one or two others as to the conditions which they found almost a century ago when they made their first journey across the prairies. There is no doubt that a very large part of Saskatchewan and Alberta is subject to recurring drought. That has been known for many years.
I would agree also with the criticism which has been made in the discussion this afternoon that it was a mistake to open up all of that country for wheat growing or cereal production. Without question large areas of it should have been reserved for ranching, for which, generally speaking, it was naturally well adapted.
The possibilities of drought received early attention. I can recall, because I have lived in western Canada for a good many years, that the popular conception in the nineties, of last century, was that the great part of southern Saskatchewan was not adapted for grain growing and never would be. That is the view which was held at that time, and it was the view, I think, which was held originally by those who had to do with the building of the first transcontinental railway, because the first survey of that railway, on the engineering reports available, placed the line a great deal further north than the location where the Canadian Pacific railway was finally constructed.
As I have said, droughts have recurred frequently. If we study the rainfall in western Canada we find that, taking Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, probably the heaviest annual rainfall is in the Red river valley, where it amounts to about twenty-one inches per annum. The rainfall gradually lessens as you move westward until in the western part of Saskatchewan and the eastern part of Alberta-I am speaking of their more southern parts, what is now referred to as the drought area-the rainfall runs from twelve to thirteen inches, and in an exceptional year to probably fourteen or fifteen inches. Now, if the rainfall is well distributed and comes at the right time, you get crops; if it is not well distributed as to season, then you have a certain amount of drought, and consequent failure of crops. That was all recognized a great many years ago, when as far back as 1894 the first Irrigation Act was passed by the federal parliament relating to the drought

Drought Area-Mr. Crerar
areas of what was then the Northwest Territories. Under that act the ownership and control of the water available in western Canada was reserved for public control, and those rights, I understand, passed to the provinces when the natural resources were transferred some seven or eight years ago.

So all the data as to the volume of water and rate of flow in these streams is to-day available in the department here or in the provincial departments having to do with the matter.
There are three sources of supply for water for the agriculturists in western Canada, or, shall we say, in the drought area. There is first the subsurface water; that is the water
which is secured from digging or drilling wells, and the like. The information on that was fragmentary and incomplete. In 1935 my right hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bennett), when he was in charge of the administration of this country- and I think this was one of the really good things he did-appropriated a very considerable sum of money to have a survey made. As a result, under the geological department of the mines branch, a survey was made of all the municipalities from the international boundary in Saskatchewan as far north as township 33. That was almost two hundred miles. That information has been plotted by the geologists and is available to any farmer in the municipalities surveyed who wishes to obtain it. It gives useful data on the water possibilities, and that data is being taken advantage of to-day in the rehabilitation program which is being carried out in those provinces as far as water supplies are concerned.
The next source of water is the ordinary spring freshet. The snow or rain falls over the vast prairies and eventually the water runs off.
The next source is that which comes from the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains or the foothills of the Rockies. There we find the origin of the great rivers of western Canada. A number of these rivers come down in the province of Alberta almost from the international boundary right to the northern section and they find their way into the two forks of the great Saskatchewan river. Some of these waters are international. That is to say, we have a stream rising in the United States, flowing into Canada and finding its way ultimately into the Saskatchewan. We have other cases where a stream rises in Canada and flows into the United States. We have one case where the river rises in the United States and flows approximately one hundred miles in Alberta, finding its way back again into the United States. So far as these streams are concerned, their use is regulated by international treaty, and Canada cannot *take more water from them than she is by treaty entitled to take.
As a result of the conditions obtaining in these western provinces some irrigation projects have been undertaken, but before discussing that phase of the subject perhaps I had better complete the point I was making. These streams have all been measured. Information regarding the total volume of water, the average over a great many years, is available, and consequently with that information in hand it is quite a practicable matter to estimate the extent of land that

could be irrigated by means of the water which can be made use of. In that respect the information asked for by my hon. friend in his resolution is, I submit, available for all practical purposes.
In consequence of the drought conditions in some of these areas irrigation projects have been undertaken and I would refer to these very briefly for a moment or two. There is one project known as the Alberta Railways Irrigation Company. That was southeast of Lethbridge and was designed to irrigate 130,000 acres.

Yes; in the case of the Lethbridge Northern the province guaranteed the bonds. Some of these have done very well. It bears out the view that where you select your area carefully, where your water can be put on at a reasonable cost, where there are farmers who will take the trouble to learn how to handle an irrigation project, you can attain a very considerable measure of success. Probably the most successful of these is the one adjacent to Lethbridge. There, as a result of irrigation, they are engaged in a type of quite intensive farming, producing sugar beet and alfalfa, and unquestionably they are getting good results.
During the years I have mentioned other projects were surveyed by the dominion government when it had charge of the lands in western Canada. Preliminary surveys were completed on these. There was one known as the Lethbridge Southeastern. There were in that 315,000 acres and the estimated cost- I would direct the attention of the house to these figures particularly-was over $40 an acre.
There were several others, including finally one known as the North Saskatchewan project. That project contemplates the diversion of the waters of the North Saskatchewan river somewhere west of Prince Albert, bringing them down over the countryside of which

Drought Area-Mr. Crerar
the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) spoke this afternoon, to irrigate the lands lying beyond. They hoped in that scheme to embrace some 1,410,000 acres but the cost would be about $75 an acre. There is no question that engineering science could solve the problem of irrigation. As an engineering question it is not an impossible thing I suppose to take the waters of lake Superior and put them on the prairies of Saskatchewan. But it has to be regarded also from the practical point of view. I ask the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar or any other hon. member, Is it a practical thing to burden land with $75 capital cost an acre to put water on it and the management expense, on top of that, and then expect farmers to carry it?

speechtext: Does the minister cite that figure of $75 an acre as a general figure?

subtopic: DESIRABILITY OF WATER CONSERVATION, IRRIGATION AND OTHER PROJECTS FOR REHABILITATION
speechtext:
No; this is just in that particular case. The figures run from $35 to $75 an acre. That gives a general picture of these projects. In the surveys made by the water powers branch at that time-and they were very complete surveys-they estimated that if all the water were utilized, probably 7,000,000 acres at the outside might be irrigated. Understand, that is all the water coming from the mountains. But that again is an impossibility. These small projects, where you can get the water on the land cheaply, are practicable propositions; but on the scale spoken of by the hon, member for Rosetown-Biggar this afternoon, taking the water, say of the South Saskatchewan river and pushing that water down, let. us say to Estevan, that, I think, is a wholly impossible proposition. In the first place the banks of the Saskatchewan river are from 100 to 300 feet high, practically all the way from Medicine Hat on. The water would have to be lifted that height from the river before the diversion over the land began. In the second place there are important cities along that river. Lethbridge gets its water supply from a tributary of the Saskatchewan river, and the town of Medicine Hat, with a population of 10,000 or 12,000 people, gets its water supply from the Saskatchewan river. Saskatoon, farther down, with a population of 45,000, gets its whole water supply from the Saskatchewan river, and my information is that they have no other source to depend upon than that. Consequently, if the waters of the river were lifted and sent over the prairies as far as Estevan, you would have the problem of the water supply for these towns and cities.
There is also another aspect of the matter which might bring about complications. The
*51952-43
South Saskatchewan is an interprovincial river. It is an important tributary of lake Winnipeg! If we could conceive it possible to divert all the waters of that river west of Prince Albert, Manitoba would be at once interested, because that would have an important effect on lake levels in Manitoba and on works which would be affected thereby. I need not say what effect it would have on areas lying east of Prince Albert.
I think the facts I have given are sufficient to indicate certain conclusions: First, that there is to-day a complete body of information available along the lines suggested in the resolution of the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar. In the second place extensive surveys have been made as to the possibility of utilizing the water available for irrigation in Saskatchewan and Alberta. May I say in passing that these reports indicate that of the acreage which could possibly be benefited by irrigation over ninety per cent is in Alberta. So that if we look for relief in undertaking vast and costly schemes of irrigation on the prairies I am afraid we are doomed to disappointment. That, however, does not mean that in certain localities' irrigation projects cannot be undertaken, but such projects must be on a modest scale such as those being undertaken to-day, which are situated almost entirely in Alberta.
I may then be asked the question, How are you going to deal with this problem? I do not think it can be dealt with in any other way than that which is being followed to-day. We may not have reached perfection by any means in the work carried on under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. But, as I have already stated, under the initiative of my right hon. friend opposite, that survey was undertaken of all the municipalities in southern Saskatchewan. The results of that survey are available. Also under the prairie farm rehabilitation scheme dams are being built to conserve the water as the snow melts in the spring and hold it. That scheme can be extended at but a fraction of the cost which would be involved in diverting the Saskatchewan river to the prairies of Saskatchewan, if that were a physical possibility. With these go the suggestions made by the hon. member for Swift Current (Mr. Bothwell) who made,
I thought, a very practical speech to-day, as well as did the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) in relation to this whole problem. There is no doubt that improved methods of farming can be found that will be of benefit to the agriculturists in these drought stricken areas. We know that progress is being made. There is hardly any limitation to what science can do. Crested wheat grass,



Drought Area-Mr. Crerar	_____
a plant which is very strongly drought resistant, has been mentioned this afternoon. With improved knowledge and the application of that knowledge to agricultural practice in these provinces, along with the work being done under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation^ Act, will be found the best road to the alleviation of the unfortunate conditions of recent years.
One point more and I am finished. I have lived in western Canada practically all my life. It has been my good fortune to be pretty well acquainted with our vast prairie country. There are not many parts of it that I have not visited at one time or another. I know its possibilities. It is true that in the last several years it has been sorely stricken. On top of the misfortune of drought, there was, owing to general world conditions, a time of low prices which further aggravated the situation as far as our farmers were concerned. But I still have faith in western Canada. In 1928, only ten years ago, the wheat fields of the prairie provinces contributed 540,000,000 bushels of wheat to the grain production of Canada, and of that amount over 300,000,000 bushels came from Saskatchewan.
I am convinced that those days will return and that western Canada once more will come into its own. I regret to see the picture painted in the dark, gloomy colours my hon. friends sometimes use in the house. We want to look at facts fairly and squarely, but there is nothing to be gained by giving the impression to the whole of Canada, and indeed to the whole world, that unless we spent hundreds of millions of dollars in irrigation projects, the country is gone and will never come back. I do not believe that. I think it will come back. What is needed to-day is a sane, sensible, practical method of going at the difficulty, and I believe that is what the government is doing in the projects whicn it is carrying on so well under the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner).

This tract includes the largest concentrated area of irrigable land in the project. The topographical and soil conditions vary greatly, but generally the lands are from smooth to gently rolling, and the soil generally a light clay loam. Throughout the southern portion in the vicinity of Elrose and Rosetown, from

To the north of township 30 the lands are generally a little more rolling, becoming distinctly rolling toward the western limit where the Bear hills commence. This area is drained by Eagle Hill creek and its various branches. To the west of Eagle Hill creek there is good slope, but to the east some of the lands are flatter and may require drainage. Several speakers have spoken of dugouts, and I know they are exceedingly valuable in northeastern Saskatchewan, and have been for ten years or more. They have been using dugouts, for example, to hold water from the spring run-off, and were it not for that factor many of my neighbours and many people in the constituency I have the honour to represent, would not have had any water

for their farm requirements last year. Even up there they were hauling water quite a considerable distance. One contractor near where I live has put in one hundred dugouts a year, and when my hon. friend speaks of high class engineering necessary to dig a dugout and that it takes a day and a half to do so, I might tell him that a man thoroughly familiar with the business and equipped with the proper machinery can put in a dugout in eleven hours. But these dugouts of which f. speak have been put in at the expense of the farmers themselves, and some of them are beginning to think that if there is to be a great deal of assistance given in building dams and dugouts and other means of conserving water elsewhere, then some assistance should be given in northern Saskatchewan and Manitoba because they feel that with the low prices they have received, with the high cost of operation and development, and with the high cost of replacements, some assistance should be given them if it is to be given elsewhere.
Valuable as this resolution might prove to be if it succeeded in inducing the government to do something that had never been done before, it is not of very great value, I think, in view of conditions as we know them as far back as sixteen or twenty years ago. But I plead with you, Mr. Speaker, and every member of the house, to give serious thought to preserving the timber on the eastern slope of the Rocky mountains, because if that goes, the control of the water goes too, and then there will be no wild life, no hunting or fishing, no possible source of water for irrigation or any other purpose, and the great cities that have been built on the rivers will find themselves in a most difficult situation. The timber of north and northeastern Saskatchewan, and Manitoba, and probably of Alberta as well, will also be in danger, and the new fur farms which have been developed in northern Saskatchewan and northwest Manitoba will also be in danger because it is no good putting in dams to hold back water if the water does not exist. But, Mr. Speaker, I am satisfied that moisture is going to come again from the clouds; that the rain will fall and the sun will shine, and the grass and wheat grow in western Canada, and no man is doing his country a service who weakens confidence in its resources of soil and climate and in the likelihood of Providence again favouring us with rainfall and sunshine in due season, which I myself am satisfied we shall have in the future.
